utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] We will resume our hearing. Counsel for the Prosecution, the floor is yours. Could you please at this point tell us the circumstances regarding protection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My colleague Miss McHenry will be taking the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. Theresa McHenry for the Prosecution. This witness has indicated about the protection previously afforded him and, therefore, we would ask that other than the address the protective order be lifted with respect to this witness who is Ibro Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Ms. McHenry, the court notes your request that you have presented regarding the protection conditions for this particular witness, and would like to give you a favourable answer to your request. So we agree fully that the next witness -- please tell us once again his identity but not his address -- that person can be introduced, brought into the session room according to the circumstances which you have just described, i.e. not concealed either in terms of his face or in terms of identification, so please introduce the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Ibro Osmanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Please would you bring the next witness in? IBRO OSMANOVIC called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Would you give the witness the headphones? Can you hear me

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] You can hear me? Mr. Ibro Osmanovic, first of all, please read out the solemn statement, the solemn oath, which has to be presented. It is on the document which is in front of you on your desk, I would presume. Please go ahead and read the oath, the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness is supposed to read it in the Bosnian language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Excuse me, would you repeat your question? Yes, I think he has to read it out in his language. Is the statement, is the declaration, the oath, in the three languages? So please would he read it out in his mother tongue, of course, quite clear so that he is quite aware and fully conscious of what he is reading. So please read out the solemn declaration in your language, the Bosnian language. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you. Sit down. Be seated. Before you start your testimony, Mr. Osmanovic, could I say to you that on behalf of the Tribunal we value very highly the fact that you are here. We are quite aware of the courage you are showing in coming here. The court would like to say to you, the Tribunal, that you are in an institution based on justice and that please feel serene during your testimony and please rely on the protection of this institution o international justice. If at any time at all during your testimony, during your statements, you find any difficulty of whatever nature, please do not hesitate to communicate that to the Tribunal. So, madam counsel for the Prosecution, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. (To the witness): Sir, would you please tell your Honours your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Ibro Osmanovic. I am from Vlasenica. I was born on 5th August 1965 and I am the citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. My nationality is Bosnian and my religion is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the war how were you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war I used to work at the SOUR "Sipad", DIP "10th August" Vlasenica company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that you were born in Vlasenica. How long had you lived in Vlasenica before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my birth, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I have an exhibit which I would like put on the computer. Maybe Mr. Dixon could help with respect to the computer? We are waiting for the exhibit to come up on the TV screen. Mr. Osmanovic, I am going to ask you that you look at what is on your computer screen. In fact, I am going to ask if you can look at the original which is where Mr. Dixon is. In fact, Mr. Dixon, could you give the witness the pen in case he at some point wants to use that as a picture? First, Mr. Osmanovic, do you recognise what that exhibit is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the panorama of the town of Vlasenica take from the Muslim cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where this picture is from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The photographs come -- the photograph comes from Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the photograph comes from or, in other words, where was this photograph found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The photograph was found in Tuzla, in the Mining Institute of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the approximate time period that this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably around 1985.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph of being a fair and accurate panorama of what Vlasenica looked like in approximately 1985?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a very fair picture. This is a view of the city from the Muslim cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. Could you use your pointer and show us some of the buildings, the important buildings, and the important sites that you recognise on this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can do that. This is the post office, the main post office. Next to it is the hotel, the police station, the municipal building, municipal authority building, a housing block, the circle road leading to Sarajevo, the medical centre in Sarajevo -- in Vlasenica, the church, the headquarters of the Energoinvest Company, the housing block in the centre of the town, the mosque, the industrial zone and Muslim cemetery. These are the locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back for a minute. When you have referred to the hotel, can you point out that again

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. The hotel was located here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the Panorama Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you point out the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is the SUP building here, next door to the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war where did you live, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived at Omladinska Street, No. 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Susica camp, Susica area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You cannot see Susica on the photograph, but here it will be behind the secondary school between the two hills, between the two hills under the Javor mountain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unless your Honours have any question with respect to this exhibit, I am finished with this exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] No questions. MISS McHENRY (To the witness): Mr. Osmanovic, can you describe what, if anything, happened in Vlasenica in approximately April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April 1992 the occupation of Vlasenica was occupied between 21st of April and 23rd April. This was done on Tuesday. It was a Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened during the occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The forces of the Yugoslav National Army, JNA, the Sremska Mitrovica and the Novi Sad Corps, they were armoured vehicles. They had occupied the vital services, and started collecting weapons both legally and illegally owned by the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe how they collected the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were collecting the weapons by inviting people through the public address system. People were given a ultimatum. They were told to hand in the weapons. If the weapons were not handed in, the JNA would use force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that the motorized unit of the Novi Sad Corps was involved; how did you know it was the Novi Sad Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met a soldier from Bijelo Polje. His name was Predrag. He said that he was serving Sremska Mitrovica and, according to the system of organisation, the whole Yugoslavia was divided into military districts. Novi Sad belonged under the Belgrade district so the Novi Sad Corps was responsible for the lower units such as Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the Novi Sad part of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the Novi Sad Corps, were there any local citizens of Vlasenica involved in the takeover and occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The local Serbs were involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that because you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. During the first two days they carried arm bands, white arm bands, and actually on the day of occupation they all emerged into the streets with white arm bands around their arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were weapons handed over by the Muslim population after the ultimatum was given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the ultimatum was given people actually had three collection points at the police station, at the medical centre and in front of the Hall of Culture, and it was only the Muslims who handed in their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They did, in fact, hand in all their weapons, is that correct, to your knowledge

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you own any weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you involved in any sort of military forces or armed resistance either before or after the occupation and takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the occupation of Vlasenica there was no armed resistance at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time after the takeover in late April or early May when a friend of yours, Dragisa Milakovic, showed you something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragisa Milakovic showed me a list and I was listed there under item 194. These were the people who were accused or suspected by the Serb community of Vlasenica to own weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go back a little bit and can you explain the circumstances under which you saw this list? Can you just tell us what happened such that you were able to see this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the evening/late afternoon, Dragisa Milakovic, my good friend otherwise, came to me. He came in his car. He hooted in front of my house. I came down. I sat into his car. He turned on the light inside the car, and showed me the list and told me to look at No. 194. When I looked at No. 194, this was my name. My brothers were not listed. The title, the heading, of this was people illegally owning weapons, and all people who I could see on the list were my well known people, people that I knew, and they were all of Muslim nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time were there any restrictions on your abilit to move around Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was the curfew. Curfew was imposed. After 9 o'clock in the evening you could not move, but leaving the city, leaving the town, was restricted and you only could go out with a pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever obtain a pass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A pass for leaving the Opstina of Vlasenica I never received, but I was given a pass to travel between my house and my land or farm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the Opstina Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the town itself, in the district where I lived I could go to my farm called Bregovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could go to your farm only because you had a pass; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who issued the passes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The passes were issued by the Crisis Headquarters of the Serbian commune of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to show the witness what has been marked for identification purposes as Exhibit 3. I do have copies of this for your Honours. (Handed) Maybe Mr. Dixon could help put that on the screen? (To the witness): Sir, I am going to ask you to look at that and tell me if you recognise what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise this is the pass such as was issued by the Serbian commune of Vlasenica for local movement within the municipality, and a similar pass, a similar pass, was given when you had to leave the Opstina of Vlasenica, but then it was handwriting down at the bottom it says: “Fo Tuzla", for instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is not your pass, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not. It is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But other than the name and the location it is similar to the pass that you received; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This pass is in the Bosnian Serbo Croatian language; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know the quality of what you have is not good, but can you please tell us as best you can what the pass says word for word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it says like this: "On the basis of Article 3 of the decision on the immediate war danger, the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica, the Crisis Headquarters, issues this pass for", the name is not written there, "from Vlasenica, for movement on the territory of the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica. The notified person has no obstacle for moving to Luka and Susica", the Head of the Crisis Headquarters, Stanic Milenko, but it was written procura by R. Matic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I am finished with that exhibit. In addition to restrictions on your movements, were there any restrictions placed on access to any financial assets you had at banks, for instance, money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a limit of 5,000 dinars so you could cash only 5,000 dinars from your account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about what you know about who passed this limit on withdrawal of money and against whom it was enforced

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came to the bank to withdraw money, I was given only 5,000 dinars -- that was the five billion dinars at that time -- while my friend, a Serb, from the same company had no restriction whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Excuse me, how much is 5,000 dinars worth? Could you answer that question, if possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] 5,000 dinars at that time was roughly 100 German marks, less than a German mark. 80 German marks, let us say, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the Novi Sad Corps left Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went about mid May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what you saw with respect to their departure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They left. The men left but all the material remained behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the men left", you mean the JNA soldiers from the Novi Sad Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the material stayed", can you explain exactly what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By "material", I have in mind armoured vehicles and tanks that were located in the town while they were there, and the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this material, the armoured vehicles and weapons, that the Novi Sad Corps and the JNA had brought with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to that equipment when they left it there? Who was given access to that equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the equipment was given to the local people, loca Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, did there come a time when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us about what happened when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I was detained was when I asked for a pass to leave the territory of the Vlasenica municipality in the direction of Tuzla. I had to go to the police station, and I saw Ljuban Stanisic. I had to be interrogated by him for this. I had to have an interview with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened during your interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the interview on the premises of the police station and the criminal service, I was shown the same list that I had been shown before by Dragisa Milakovic. They asked me where the weapon was that I had, and I said I did not know and they asked Mr. Milakovic to come, that he would explain. He came. He gave some sort of guarantee and I was released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back for a minute. When you say they asked if you owned a weapon, did you tell them that you did not know where the weapon was or did you tell them that you did not have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was asked about my weapons and about the weapons of some neighbours of mine, if they had any weapons, if I knew about the whereabouts of these weapons and I said I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say with respect to the weapons that you were alleged to have

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weapons that I was accused of having and the weapons about my neighbours, I said I had absolutely no knowledge of any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it that Mr. Milakovic was called in to give a guarantee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was called in because I asked him, I asked for him to be called in because he knew me because I was his good friend. About 70 per cent of my free time I spent with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time how was Mr. Milakovic working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Milakovic before the war had worked as a teacher of biology and chemistry in the Elementary School of Milici. During the war, during the days of the occupation and on, he issued passes for moving around the municipality and he was working at a checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, he had an official position within the Serb administration that was administering Vlasenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Mr. Milakovic gave his guarantee on your behalf, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He explained to me the man who had worked at the police station in this particular area issuing documents in case of my forceful illegal exit from town that I would be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went home, and I was arrested again on 22nd May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back, to your knowledge, between the time of your first and second arrest, do you know if there was any armed conflict or attacks in the area surroundin Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vlasenica itself there was no fighting, but in the area around Vlasenica some Muslim villages were set on fire such as Bare Dzamdzici, Pijuci, which meant that people would come from these villages into the town, that everything had been burnt down. They had no place to go back to and there are many dead people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, do you know about who committed these attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the names of the people who commanded these actions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not they were military forces or do you know whether or not they were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were military forces because everybody was in military uniforms and also the JNA uniforms as well as the local people were wearing uniforms too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what happened when you were arrested on 22nd May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 22nd May in the afternoon I was taken from my house to the police station to make a statement. However, I did not make a statement, but I was arrested instead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I go back, where were you at the time that you were arrested when someone first came to get you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no arrest warrant when I was first detained, and there was no arrest warrant the second time either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that there was no arrest warrant? Did you ask for one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked Bastah Dragan. He said that there was no need for a warrant arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about now 22nd May

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you were told that they did not need an arrest warrant? What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was escorted out of my house, under threat of attack. I was put in the vehicle owned -- a Golf -- owned by the police station of Vlasenica. There were some other local Serbs there who also got into the car. I was the only Muslim in the car. I was taken to the police station. 9 Q. Were the local Serbs in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man who came to collect me had camouflage uniform on, and the others were in the uniforms of the reserve forces of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you brought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to the SUP, to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you went to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I was detained I was taken to the office of the criminal service, but I was then -- there was a detour made and I was put in the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain the difference between those two locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The criminal service office was the office where they interrogated people. But within the SUP premises they made a prison, which was remodeled from a form of toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened to you next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found people there in that prison, all of them Muslims. They took us out, starting the 22nd May until the 2nd June, they took us out to the office of the criminal service. They beat some of them; others they interrogated and beat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was personally beaten, abused, physically abused, interrogated, and I was asked where the artillery weapon called "Zis" was in my location, in my area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened to you during the beatings? How were the beatings conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maltreatment was carried out in the following way: First, they would open the door of the detention facility where we were. They would point with their finger and say: "You, you and you". Sometimes they would take out one individual, sometimes two. The room where the interrogation took place, there were two chairs and a table. When we entered that room our hands were bound to the table, and our chests would be against the back of the chair, and our feet were tied to the legs of the chair. We were stripped to the waist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what would happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they started beating us. They used various objects to beat us, starting with the ordinary truncheon, police truncheon, various poles and even sticks and even chains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were in that location, the prison, can you estimate approximately how many times you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was beaten about five times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any injuries from your beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have injuries from Zoran Obrenovic on the legs, on my arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Zoran Obrenovic one of the people who was beating you while you were at the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not Zoran Obrazoviv but Zoran Obrenovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he inflict those injuries on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was maltreated in the following way: He forced me to spread out my fingers and stuck the point of his blade between my -- the knife between my fingers and I had scars and also in the area of my knee he stuck his knife into my knee. He said, whatever he asked me, I did not know what to answer because I knew I would be hit, and the third -- the third time I hit in the leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were hit with the knife on the leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After the injury, they put salt not only on my wound but all the others. They put salt on the wound.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] What were the questions they put to you? What questions did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] The questions they asked me were who armed the Muslims? Who prepared the uprising against Serbs? Where is the canon, Zis? Do I know of my neighbour, Mensusmic(?), or the people who were active in the Muslim party?

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Had there been an uprising against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vlasenica itself there was no rebellion. People were organised in the territory of Srpske, Kalesije, Tuzla and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they asking you about what happened in Vlasenica or what happened in those other areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We knew that there was armed resistance. Before I was arrested the television showed the battlefield in Kalesije and also some of what happened in Tuzla on 15th May. We knew about Srebrenica, but I was asked exclusively about the canon, and about the people from the Muslim party who had weapons, who sold weapons, the Muslim people for armed resistance against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you being asked about people in Vlasenica or peopl in other areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked me about people in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone was killed during this time in the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly what you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dzemal Ambeskovic was killed, a retired policeman, traffic policeman, for the area of Zvornik and he had lived in the Omladinska Street at No. 13; father of three children, aged about 50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was brought to the cell completely deformed, his face completely deformed and swollen from beating, and with a swollen stomach, a very swollen stomach. He was called out by Stevan Mumovic, opened the door for him and as soon as he got out we could hear a shot, first a hit and then a shot. After that Garic and Mumovic came in and asked us to take his body out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did take his body down to, and put it on a vehicle of the make of Tam owned by the fire brigade of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the building, the prison building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that building I remained until June 2nd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On June 2nd where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that date I was taken to the municipal prison in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how it was that you were transferred to the municipal prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken on foot. They took me on foot because it was not far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why you were transferred to the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I say I do not know really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you were at the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to the prison on the 2nd June. I was put in cell No. 1, and I was taken out of this cell on the same day. I was beaten, brought back to my cell, then they listed -- the list was made of people who had been to this cell or who were, in fact, brought in as they were brought in because more people were brought in and they were placed into these cells. That was done during the night, and 22 people were taken out of my cell during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The beating that you have just referred to, was this the only beating you received when were you at the municipal prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was more maltreatment, but that was between the 2nd June and 18th June. I had been taken out on a number of occasions and all kinds of experiences I had from that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us something about those experiences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maltreatment in this prison was conducted in the following way: We would be brought to a toilet at the other end of the corridor from the main entrance. Then we would be asked to put our hands on the window, to spread our legs a far as possible, so that we were totally exposed with our ribs and the waist and this was all exposed for easier beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you, in fact, then be beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they would beat us with their feet, with batons, with rifle butts, with the whole submachine guns, with the bod of the submachine gun. Then all kinds of metal bars would be used, sticks, thick plastic pipes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any injuries from these beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five teeth -- I lost five teeth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the prison were you ever taken out to do any work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were forced to do all kinds of things. Everything was done by force, first of all, robbing Muslim houses, loading different kinds of materials on to vehicles, then digging trenches on the battle front, arranging the battle front, then burying the dead and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of your work were you ever sent to Drum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what kind of work and what you observed when you were sent to Drum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to Drum, were taken by -- in a vehicle, in a lorry, and in front of the cafe at the exit from Drum to Piskavica we found the bodies of 22 people of different ages between 18 and 55.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these people such that you could tell where they were from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they from? Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were from Drum. They were the local villages, local residents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know their ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their ethnic origin was Bosniac, Muslims by religion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any wounds or injuries that might have indicated how these 22 people died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of those that we buried, the 22 people, had injurie from firearms and they were shot in their forehead and one of them, Hodzic, had the chest riddled with bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What work did you actually do at Drum with these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We buried the bodies. We first put them on a tractor, took them to the Muslim cemetery where we were asked to take all their belongings, money, documents and any jewellery they had on. The trench was already dug. We put lime first and then a dredger was used to actually pile earth on the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left the municipal prison on June 18th where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the municipal prison we were taken on 18th May to the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "Susica camp", had Susica always been a camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war the sheds in Susica were owned by the forestry company of Bihac -- that is the forest management company; that was part of the Sipad group of companies -- and then at one point the territorial army used those sheds to store their territorial defence unit weapons. Also they had some training grounds there for young people. Then some five or six years before the war an additional hangar was built for the needs of the territorial defence units, and in that hangar we were then housed or detained.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the help of the clerk and Mr. Dixon, I would like to show the witness what has previously been marked for identification purposes as Exhibit 2. (Handed) (To the witness): Sir, do you recognise what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the drawing showing the Susica camp

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Using the pointer, can you explain the diagram to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Susica camp is this area, it is actually situated on the locality of the Vlasenica, Han Pijesak, Pale road. Then there is the road leading into the forest. That is the dirt road. This is where the camp was located, along that road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point out and explain to us what the various markings within the camp are and if they are not exactly accurate would you please tell us how you believe the camp was set out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Susica camp, there were two hangars there. You see the two warehouses. In the first one, we had the various kinds of equipment, military materials. We had to load this. This was the sentry point. This is the River Susica which gave the name to the camp. This is a toilet with 10 cubicles, and this hangar would be about one third to the right, I think, one third of the way to the right. There was also a machine gun in placement, and this is the electricity pole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Sorry, what are the two small buildings, the outbuildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This building -- in the north, yes, yes, this ... I do not know what this is. I have no idea. I know that this was moved a bit higher. This building was further away from the fence and the fence was just along the bank of the river while the entrance was on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who the commander of Susica prison was

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the Susica camp was Dragan Nikolic nicknamed Jenki.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know he was the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived, when we were brought to the Susica camp, he was the one that we had to approach when we were taken out to work, when we were -- even when we wanted to leave for the toilet. Anything who came to the camp addressed him and he himself actually confirmed his status using the words, well, at one time he shot over the hangar, he said: "I am here, God, the stick and the law".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In his role as commander, what relationship did you observe between Dragan Nikolic and the guards at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Relations between Dragan Nikolic and the camp guards was a typical, typically more than friendly. There was no strict hierarchy of superior subordinate but, on the other hand, the guards were not allowed to do anything without his approval.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in other words, it was a friendly relationship but he approved whatever the guards did; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute ago you said Dragan Nikolic shot over the hangar and said he was God, the stick and the law. What do you mean when you say "he shot over the hangar"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was shooting the height above, two metres above the ground while we were seated, so he was shooting over our heads just to intimidate us and frighten us, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Dragan Nikolic before you were at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you know about him before you arrive at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew about him before that, that he was employed at the Alpro Company, the Bauxite Company, in Vlasenica Aluminium Moulds. I used to see him in Vlasenica in town before the war, of course. I know that his brother was employed in the municipal administration. One of his relatives was employed with me in my factory, and on the day of the occupation of Vlasenica Dragan Nikolic was a member of the military police, special military police units, the so-called special military police units of the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica, as they called themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Susica, can you estimate how many other detainees there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we entered the hangar I would say there were between 500 and 550 people altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many men there were versus how many women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were only eight women.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Can you say what was the size, what was the volume, of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hangar was about 15 metres wide and some 30 metres long.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How much room therefore -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just a clarification: Mr. Nikolic was in the 25 special military police unit. Was this part of the Serbian army or the local police unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was part of the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know with respect to your fellow detainees their ethnic origin or religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them were Bosniacs and all of them were Muslim b religion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not any of these people were involved in the military or had been involved in armed resistance against the Serb takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know of anybody who had been involved in that way, I mean, because there was no armed resistance in Vlasenica and there was nobody to take part in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was everyone that you knew at the camp a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for people from Vlasenica, all of them were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe generally what conditions were like at the camp and by that I mean how crowded it was, what kind of food or sanitary conditions there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said there were some 500, 550 people altogether. We were placed on a concrete floor. Some people from Vlasenica who were brought when the camp was first established had brought with them some blankets, so they actually spread on their blankets, but the rest of us had to sleep on the concrete floor. The toilet was allowed only in the morning and in the evening, and we would be sent out in group of 50, and during the night there was a pail in a corner which was about volume of 10 litres and you could then urinate there. The food was brought once a day irregularly around 11 o'clock. It was rather cold. It was rainy. We were greatly overcrowded. The windows were closed. We did not have enough oxygen to breathe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much food did you receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We used to get food once a day. It was around 11 o'clock, as I said, and the food, as far as the quality -- quantity was concerned, was enough to feed a child; there was very little food

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there another detainee at the camp named Durmo Handzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Handzic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Durmo Handzic before you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Durmo Handzic. He was a retired worker from the Bauxite Company of the Energoinvest Group from Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how old would you estimate Mr. Handzic was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 60 and 65, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also a detainee named Asim Zildzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Asim Zildzic was also in that camp. I found him there when I arrived. He was the retired worker of the Sipad group companies, 10th August company. He was about 50 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you see happen to Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic at Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything happen to Mr. Handzic and Mr. Zildzic while you were at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zildzic and Mr. Handzic were taken out. They were beaten. They were brought back to the cell. Zildzic died one night, and Durmo died the following morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you remember going back first when they were called out? First of all, do you remember approximately when this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That happened about 24th May. Between 22nd and 24th June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of the day was it approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the evening, they were taken out in the evening, the first time, and beaten and they were returned to the hangar, and before that they had been interrogated in the office

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back. When they were called out, do you know who called them out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic called them out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us in as much detail as you remember everything that happened starting from the time that Dragan Nikolic called them out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the moment of their exit until they returned, we did not see what happened to them, but we heard screams, the moaning, of these people. After they returned to the hangar they had to take Asim out and Durmo staggered and managed to reach the place that was assigned for him to sleep in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time they were called out and then they were outside, could you hear whether or not they were being asked any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the camp they were asked questions in the hangar, but I did not hear questions once they were taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What questions did you hear them ask when they were in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hangar they asked Durmo Handzic where his son was, who was employed by the territorial Defence of Vlasenica prior to the occupation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was asking Mr. Durmo these questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question was asked by Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Durmo Handzic able to answer Dragan Nikolic's questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He answered by saying: "I do not know".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after he said he did not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he took him out again in the morning when he came back. When Asim Zildzic died he told him decidedly: “Yo see, Durmo, Asim has died; will you tell me now?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are talking about this is the next morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct that you said that Mr. Zildzic after you heard screams and moans was brought back in by some other people into the hangar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the door of the hangar to his place he was carried by some people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was he carried rather than walking himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He could not walk. He had been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you observe about his condition besides that he could not walk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He could not speak. He just sobbed, kept sobbing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He died after about 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is during the night, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after he died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After he died Ferhatovic, brothers Ferhatovic, were called out to take him out, to take his body out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this during the night or the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took him out during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next morning Nikolic came, he came up to Durmo Handzic and told him decidedly: "Durmo, you see Asim has died, will you tell me now?" Durmo responded: "Dragan, let me see the sun once more." Dragan said: "No, will you tell me?" Durmo started walking towards the door without his approval, and after several metres he fell down and die -- and collapsed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then Durmo was taken out too, brothers Ferhatovic buried both Durmo and Asim as they said in the Muslim graveyard.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] With your permission, we would like to take a break for 15 minutes so we will come back and start again at 11.30. The hearing is adjourned. (Short Adjournment) (11.30 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] You have the floor to continue.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. Osmanovic, was there a detainee at Susica camp named Cice Arnaut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us everything you remember, if anything, about what you observed happened to Cice Arnaut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cice Arnaut, nicknamed Cice, the son of Rifet, was in the Susica camp together with us. He was beaten and kicked in the chest by the Dragan Nikolic. He forced him to put his head back and he put the knife of the rifle in his mouth, of his rifle, the bayonet knife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this on one occasion or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The beating was repeated several times, and I saw that he put the knife in his mouth only once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you remember about the time he put the knife in his mouth and where did it happen exactly, what did you see, was Mr. Arnaut injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Arnaut, as he had his head tossed back, Nikolic would put the rifle, the knife it was bloody at the point, and he spat out blood after that

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Arnaut spat out blood after the knife had been, the bayonet had been inside him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it that Dragan Nikolic put the bayonet in his mouth; in other words, where was Mr. Nikolic and was Mr. Arnaut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happened in the hangar, about several metres from where I was standing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dragan Nikolic ever asked Mr. Arnaut any questions while he was beating him or prior to putting the bayonet in his mouth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nikolic asked Arnaut where his brother was, nicknamed Cene, who had illegally left Vlasenica in the direction of Kladanj, and accused him of trying to rape his mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, who is accusing ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nikolic accused Cice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a detainee named Dzevad Saric at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Dzevad Saric was in the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to take us through, starting from the beginning, what, if anything, you saw happen with respect to Mr. Saric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dzevad Saric was employed by the People's Defence Secretariat prior to the occupation of the municipality of Vlasenica. He had been brought to the Susica camp. Nikolic took him out and Galib Smajlovic took them both out. When they came back Dzevad walked, but he kept quiet and was very pale, and Galib, when he came to his place, collapsed, fainted and shook heavily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We asked him when he came to, when Smajlovic came to, we asked him why he had been beaten. He said: "My man, for no reason. I was just, I was beaten for no reason whatsoever and the less you know the better for you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the night the following were taken out: Musa Zekic Dzevad Saric, Dzevad Saric and Muharem Kolarevic. After that I was taken out, but only to the door. Then I was returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I go back? When you say they were taken out, can you tell us what you remember about when they were taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the night when they left the hangar, Musa Zekic was taken out, then Saric then Kolarevic. We could hear shots first time. The second time also shots and the third time we heard screams. I raised my head after hearing the screams, and at that moment Zoran Obrenovic came to the door together with Sladan Pajic and Djuric. They asked a question, "Who has tried to escape?" Zoran Obrenovic called on me telling me, "Miki, come over here." When I came up to him he asked me who had tried to escape. I answered: "I don't know. I was asleep." Sladan Pajic grabbed me by the chest and pushed me towards the door and Kolarevic, my colleague from work, had said: "I won't give him to you. There's the hangar for you and you can pick and choose whomever you like, but I will not allow him to be taken out." I was returned to the place where I slept. I was escorted by Zoran Obrenovic. He came up to Rasid Ferhatbegovic. He kicked him and just told him: "Get out of here." After he got out there was a shot heard, and then there was silence after that. The following morning they called out: "Brothers, Ferhatbegovic" to bury those people, and the rest of us, at the eighth hour, near the eighth hour, the following morning saw blood that had come out through the sand and the blood had not been there the previous day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who came in that you referred to and initially tried to take you out, were these guards at the camp or soldiers from the outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Besides Ljubinko Djuric, he was the guard in the camp, the other two they had light camouflage uniforms on and belonged to the Unit for Special Action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the other two were not guards at the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what, if any, relationship those two people had with Dragan Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic himself was wearing the same camouflage uniform as they did, and before my arrest I had seen them around the town going together, Obrenovic, Pajic, Nikolic and many other individuals from Vlasenica that I know personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So am I correct that it was your brief that Dragan Nikolic was friends with these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] If you do not mind, a question is going to be put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to have more clarification concerning the Unit for Special Action and whether Nikolic was part of this unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] In the Former Yugoslav Army there are reconnaissance units, logistics, sabotage units whic belong to some special units, to units usually called "special". They wore generally light camouflage uniforms. They were dressed in such uniforms in Vlasenica, Obrenovic, Pajic brother, Nikolic. They brought all the people, after my arrival to the Susica camp they brought all the other inmates from the 18th until 13th June. They were the ones who collected people and brought them to the detention centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What was Nikolic's role in this unit? What was his grade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] I do not know what rank he had there, but I used to see him in front of the Crisis Headquarters which was located in the administration building of the Bauxite Company, with the insignia "Serbian Military Police", armed, I saw him armed, and after that when I came to the camp I saw him and he was the one who said: "I am here, the commander, God, the stick and the law."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know of any superiors to Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were superior to Nikolic while we were in the camps, Susica camp, there are came somebody called Kraljevic who was a lieutenant in the Yugoslav People's Army, JNA, and as soon as he arrived Nikolic tried to clean the camp, to arrange things, to put them in good order because he says "The king is coming" because he says: "Only the king can order me and nobody else", but Kraljevic has the name "kral", "king", as part of the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you have any belief about why the guard, Djuric, prevented Obrenovic and the other man from taking you

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems to me that he prevented them because we worked together. We had worked together for 10 years before the war. We were also friends after work, and even during the working hours we were together, we worked next to each other. So eight hours of our working time we spent together and were friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the time that when Obrenovic first came into the hangar yelling: "Who tried to escape?" did you do anything, to your knowledge, that led him to select you or led him or Mr. Pajic to select you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not possible to escape from the hangar, it was just impossible, because the windows were three metres above ground from the floor, the metal door was locked from the outside, and they just walked in and said: "Who has tried to escape? Close the windows, close" while nobody had even thought of escaping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that you may have made some movement that caught the attention of Djuric or Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I made a mistake because I raised my head.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] I would like to ask the witness how was the camp guarded at night? There was a shift, I suppose, permanently. What type of facilities did they take? Were there search lights? Could you give us some more details on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] The protection or the security in the camp consisted in the fact that there were guards on duty, and these were, sorry, inside the hangar there were prisoners or detainees who were called the orderlies of the day.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] The microphone is not on. I did not hear the witness's statement, I am sorry. Sir, could yo please repeat your answer and let us hope this that time technical aspects will not let us down. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] The hangar -- within the hangar there were the appointed orderlies from among the detainees, orderlies of the day. On the outside of the hangar, the gate, the main gate, was floodlit with two spot lights. The door was locked. It was a metal door. There was also barbed wire around the camp. The windows, as I already said, were very high above the floor, and there was no opportunity or no possibility, even the windows, if you wanted to climb the windows they were so small that a man could hardly go through them.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were there instances of mistreatment or abuse by Dragan Nikolic besides the ones that you have already told us about this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what, if anything, you remember about those or can you describe them in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, I personally was forced to sit for about 40 hours in water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who ordered you to sit in the water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Another detainee known as "Brizo", the nickname "Brizo", he beat that man. The two brothers Muminovic he separated, saying -- he came one night and said: "Let us take out everything that we have in our pockets" and he wanted to see all our belongings in front of us, and in the morning when he came, he came to Garli Muminovic and his brother. He found a set of tractor keys and car - and a set of car keys, and then he said: "Oh, now, you bastards, I am saving your -- I am trying to secure your wives and your children and you are hiding these things your belongings in the forest, but I found them all." Then he maltreated a woman who was a younger woman, about 20 years of age. He asked her whether she would marry another detainee who was one of us, but who was the orderly of the day, and who was actually Nikolic's friend from before the war. Then he asked another man to sell his wife to him and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever observe Dragan Nikolic trying to scare any detainees by using his pistol in some way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us what you remember about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic was armed. He had two hand grenades on him. He had pistol 7.67 millimetres, TT brand, made by the Zastava 101 Yugoslav company; he had a bayonet; he had a gas cylinder or a gas grenade and an automatic rifle calibre 7.62. Then he would come to individual people. He would cock the pistol and then pull the trigger although there was no bullet in the gun. He asked now: "What happens now if I now pull the trigger if I simply drop this grenade and suffocate you” or “you are not worth the cigarette butt". Then he shot from his automatic rifle above our heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "sometimes he would cock his pistol and then pull the trigger even though it was empty", would the pistol be pointed at anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know it cannot be easy but, as best you can, can yo describe how you felt, your psychological condition, when you were at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Susica camp I found between 500 and 550 people, eight women among them, I found my younger brother there who had been brought to the camp just a few days before me. The situation in the camp was the following: We were divided into groups and in one group we had people from the Kalesije municipality and Cekovici municipality; in the second group we had people from the Vlasenica municipality, these were larger groups, and then there were smaller groups for women; also, for some people who had just returned from the regular army service in the Yugoslav National Army, and a third smaller group was the group of people who he had separated so that they could sit by the door. During -- I mean, everybody actually during the night everybody waited for the day to come because day meant going out to work, not seeing what was happening. The maltreatment and suffering was a bit less, while the night was the night of horror.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say it was a "night of horror" why were the nights full of horror?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Durmo Handzic, for instance, Asim Zildzic were beaten during the night and Zildzic actually died during the night, as I already said. Some people were killed during the night. So, everybody who was taken out of the hangar and had never returned, that happened always during the night, and so people who were taken out and never brought back were actually taken out during the night, so the nights were nights of fear

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you afraid during the night that you might be taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were able to leave Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went out of the Susica camp accompanied by the guards, that is when we went to work outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left Susica and were transferred to another location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 30th June I was transported to the Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances by which you left Susica and were brought to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The circumstances of my departure towards Batkovic, the circumstances were the following: They would call our names. Then we went through a line up and we came to the bus. We sat on the bus and we were beaten on the way, and those who were beating us were singing the praises of the Serbian Chetniks during the war, such as Mihalovic. They said (indecipherable): "Prepare the salad; there will be meat and we will kill and slaughter the Croats". There were Serbian nationalistic songs which had been legally banned during the socialist times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the time that your names were called out at Susica and then you were put on the buses, who was involved in organising this departure, calling out the names and thing likes that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The transport was actually done on three occasions in three groups. The first group left on 27th June. That was the Kalesije group. They were told that they would be exchanged on 27th -- until the 27th June, then 30 per cent of people from Kalesije left, and then from another village people from another village, and they were also told that they would be exchanged. We were collected on 30th June. Around noon they called our names. That was Veljko Basic who called the names, but actually he received the list from Nikolic, and during all three transports, the first and second transport, Nikolic actually was the one who gave the list to Basic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the position, if any, of Veljko Basic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Veljko Basic was a retired police worker from Vlasenica, and when I was transported to Batkovic I asked Nikolic whether my brother could go with me so that we would not be separated. Nikolic said: "Ask Veljko Basic because he said he has the last word". So I went to Veljko Basic to ask but he would not allow this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this your younger brother that you said was at the camp when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was your brother permitted to go on the bus with you when you were sent to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. This was not allowed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, happened to your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw him again. We have tried through the International Red Cross. We resorted to a tracing service but without success.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to the International Red Cross, did the International Red Cross ever come to Susica camp when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 30th June then you were transferred to Batkovic; i that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you spend at Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent the time between the 30th June 1992 until the 27th July 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell your Honours approximately where the Batkovic camp was located, what part of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina it was and about how far away it was from Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Counsel for the Prosecution, could I interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] The Batkovic camp, was it or was it not led by Dragan Nikolic? I do not think it was, was it?

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Good, fine. This question then regarding the process, the actions you are taking, your office, against Dragan Nikolic, I am wondering whether we should really start talking about this particular description. You have called the witness. It is up to you. If you think it is useful to continue this explanation by the witness of his suffering, as far as I am concerned, I do not think my colleagues have any objection to this. There is no problem, I think, dealing with this one month period at the Batkovic camp. However, maybe you could explain to us very briefly the reasons why you would like to ask the witness these questions, whether or not it is useful or important regarding the accusation.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly, your Honour. With respect to the transfer to Batkovic, one of the reasons I specificall wanted to do that is because one of the counts of the indictment -- excuse me while I find exactly which one -- I believe count 22, is charging Nikolic with the unlawful transfer of civilians from Susica camp do Batkovic camp. So that is a specific count in the indictment under articles 2(g) of our Statute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] So I understand, Madam, that you intend asking questions regarding conditions in which the transfer took place?

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe that I have just generally got those conditions. The other reason I was going to ask him to describe very briefly where Batkovic was and what kind of treatment he had at Batkovic because I believe it may go to the widespread systematic nature of what happened, and then which I believe is something the Prosecutor must establish, certainly for Article 5 of our Statute. But I do not plan on going into as much detail as we have with respect to the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] I would like to ask you for a few moments. Thank you. Counsel for the Prosecution, Madam, the Tribunal is of the opinion that it is correct for you to explain the conditions of transfer which are part of the indictment, and that the witness may tell us about these conditions but more briefly regarding the Batkovic camp. The second point, which is more detailed but which we have to rectify -- this is not a detail, of course, for the witness -- I would like to ask you this, whether or not in the Batkovic camp the witness stayed there one year or one month. Could you please tell us that, make that clear

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe the witness stayed at Batkovic for one year and it is, with respect to your first point, the case that my questions about Batkovic are really directed just to showing a widespread and systematic nature as well as the sort of State action and some of those elements, so they will be very brief, as your Honour has indicated.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Let there be no misunderstanding, especially regarding the role of the witness. It is not the intention at all of the Tribunal to cut down the amount of time available to him. This is an indictment against somebody called Dragan Nikolic. We are in the Tribunal and, of course, we do not want to skirt around the issue in any way whatsoever, so perhaps I can suggest the following: You can ask questions regarding conditions for the transfer and then subsequently we could ask the witness to speak freely and at greater length if he wants to regarding the conditions of detention. That is what I would like to suggest. MISS McHENRY (To the witness): Can you tell us approximately where Batkovic is and, if you know, approximately how far you had to travel to be transferred from Susica to Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Batkovic camp was located about 10 or 12 kilometres from Bijeljina in the direction of Dvorvi, left direction, near the agriculture faculty in Bijeljina. This was the agriculture farming estate called Semberija. Bijeljina is about 100 kilometers from Vlasenica. The transport took about four or five hours because we arrived there in early evening, to Batkovic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you like, sir, can you briefly describe generally the kind of treatment you saw or experienced during your year at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The treatment in Batkovic, from the moment when we came there, we ran the gauntlet until we came into the hangar and were beaten in the process. There was a roll call in hangar one by one. We again had to go between two lines of Chetniks, were beaten and then we were placed against the wall of that hangar, and the escorts who were with us during the transportation asked us to hand over any valuables, watches, money, jewellery. They also took some leather jackets from some individual prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were led into the Batkovic camp during the year you were there did you witness or yourself experience any mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it and I suffered it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
