utterances.text: Without going into detail, can you describe generally the kinds of mistreatment you yourself experienced and the kind you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was physically abused. I was beaten, and I also saw others being beaten, and some of those who were beaten succumbed to this beating -- died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you released from Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Batkovic on 21st July in 1993 through the mediation of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no additional questions for this witness. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you. Mr. Osmanovic, are you married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you married when you were in the Susica camp

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you live with your family in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your father, mother, brothers, sisters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My -- in my family I had a mother, three sisters, two brothers, a father -- the father died before the war -- my older brother had lived in the surroundings of Vlasenica. His wife told me later that he had been killed in the Susica camp and in the Susica camp, my younger sister remained behind in the Susica camp and my younger brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your sister? Your younger sister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one sister, the youngest of the sisters, born in 1975.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Susica camp, you saw eight women there. When you arrived at the Susica camp you saw eight women there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know them before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did know the oldest woman by sight and I also knew the young woman relatively well, the youngest among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were young and old women there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they living together with the men in the same place or were they in a separate place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the area of the hangar we were altogether. The only difference was that they slept in an area where they did not come in contact with the women -- with the men, but we were in the same room, in the same hall, hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The youngest one is now in Tuzla, and the others left tha area, the Susica camp. I have not seen them since because there was a group of inmates who were taken out -- if you allow me, I can explain this. There was a group of women who were taken out of the camp and children and older people. They were taken out in an unknown direction, so that these women also left the camp together with the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they were there in the camp every day, do you know what happened at that time in second camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside the camp while we were there, during my time there from the 18th of June, another group of women was brought on 25th and children and older people and adults. They included Cica and Adana Patkovic, Enisa Topalovic. There was a girl called Lela Delic. There were parents, there were children, there were babies, people under age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to them? They were beaten, tortured, killed, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard that Lela had been raped, but we heard that when we came to Tuzla. The evening when Saric was called out, Kolarevic and Zekic, they were not in the hangar. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I understood that Nikolic did not represent the local forces but was linked to the JNA army. Is this conclusion right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what he represented, but I know he represented authority, some authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you say it was the unit for special action? He belonged to the unit for special action of the ex Yugoslav army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was a member of their unit in the area of th Vlasenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, he belonged to that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] I would also like to ask you a question: The total duration of your detention from the point of your departure from the Opstina, how many months or how many years did that last in total, please, until you came under the protection of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the day, my first day, which was the 22nd May 1992, until the 21st July 1993 -- exactly 13 months and 29 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Batkovic (and this is the only question I have about that camp), did you witness during the night, in particular, scenes similar to those that you witnessed at the Susica camp concerning, for example, Durmo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was there when they took out people, both during the day and during the night. They took out Amir Berbic whom they nicknamed "Serbo sjek" which means the cutter of Serbs; Mostacevic Nedim, whom they nicknamed "Green beret"; Alija Horseman, nicknamed "Horseman" from Bjelina Savic Djevic Zecevic, an owner of a restaurant, Hussain Smajic, the butcher from Bjelina, Edin nicknamed "builder" from Kalesije. Those are the people who were marked by them and were taken out every day on a daily basis and were beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were a number of people killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The first one to die from beating was Zulfo Hadziomerovic, a retired worker of the veterinarian station in Vlasenica; Hussain Zlatar also died; Ferid Zecevic, the man from Tersak, but I also heard that on was shot dead in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like also to ask you a different question regarding the period before the war in the village. Did you have any particular political or trade union responsibilities? Were you a member of an Islamic party? Did you belong to an association or any grouping involved at the municipal level or involved in political activities, democratically speaking, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the -- I had been a member of the league of communists of Yugoslavia which was a political organisation, and I was also a volunteer of the fire brigade, of the voluntary fire brigade in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final question, very simply, please, and speak very freely, what are the feelings that you conserve now regarding all these events which took place? What are the feelings which you presently have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went through that earlier, this is my history, my life, something I obviously could not miss.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that this testimony has now been completed so we can accompany him to the place which has been reserved for him. If he could be showed out straightaway, then we will discuss how we organise the rest of our work for the end of the morning session and then how we work this afternoon. The Tribunal thanks you for your testimony. (The witness withdrew) Counsel for the prosecution, the floor is yours. Please make to us some proposals. It is now 12.25. Normally speaking, we would finish on a daily basis at 1 o'clock. We have a very long programme of hearing until the end of next week. On the other hand, only you know whether or not it is possible to interrupt a testimony. Therefore, it is up to you to guide us in organising our discussions. So, would you suggest that we take the next witness and go on to 1 o'clock and then we come back at 2.30 with the rest, or would you prefer us to break off now and then we would start again at 2 o'clock?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours pleases, I am happy to start now. The witness is ready to come forward and give his testimony. He is presently waiting to do so. I do not think there would be any difficulty in him starting his evidence now and having it broken at 1 o'clock for the adjournment. Your Honour, in respect of the next witness that I wish to call, we have spoken to that witness and he has indicated to us that he is prepared to give his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Excuse me, counsel for the Prosecution. I would like to consult my colleagues on your proposal, if I may. Yes. Counsel for the Prosecution, the Tribunal welcomes your proposal which, of course, is so much in line with our wishes regarding the organisation of our discussions. Before you introduce the next witness, as we do for each witness, please tell us the conditions in which the next witness (whose name I will not yet reveal) wishes to make his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, we have spoken to the next witness that we propose to call. That witness has indicated to us that he is prepared to give his evidenc in public, and for that reason we seek a lifting of the non-disclosure order in respect of that witness in respect of all matters except for his address.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] The Tribunal notes your request, and can accept it, of course. The address of the following witness will not be revealed, will not be mentioned. You will be revealing to us the identity of the witness. I would like to ask the Registrar to note the request which you have made and the answer of the Tribunal, so we can introduce the next witness and you can tell us immediately the identity of that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. I call Redjo Cakisic. REDJO CAKISIC called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Cakisic, would you please read out the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] I solemnly declare that I speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Cakisic, please feel free to sit down. The Tribunal, as was the case for the other people who have come with you, would like to thank you for coming here in conditions which we know are difficult, both in terms of material considerations, physical considerations and in terms of moral considerations. Let me remind you that you appear in an international Tribunal which is a place of justice. So you are under the protection of the justice system and you can feel completely serene about your testimony. If at any time at all during your testimony yo experience any difficulties of any nature whatsoever, do not hesitate to communicate those to the Tribunal. Counsel for the Prosecution, you can begin your examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If it pleases your Honours. Is your full name Redjo Cakisic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 4th April 1957.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the municipality of Vlasenica, the village of Piskavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where had you lived for most of your life prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in my native village in Piskavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you spend a period of time doing service in the army of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I served in the JNA. For 15 months I was drafted and when I finished my years of service, then I was kept on the reserve list for 10 years and I was called up for military exercises every year, once a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do your military service in the years 1976 to 1978?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the period -- I cannot give you the -- I served that I was in the -- I was regularly drafted. I was a conscript and as soon as I was released they put me on the reserve unit so that we would then have yearly exercises for 15 days, 10 to 15 days, so I went for about 10 years each year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now ask you to cast your mind back, if you would, until just immediately prior to June 1992 and if you coul tell me your recollections of the events around about that time in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you that, I can tell you how I was detained, how I was captured and taken to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Please do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked at the beginning of the war, I worked in the forestry company and I went to my work on a daily basis until the 2nd June. On 2nd June I went to work that morning. I was waiting for the bus in front to take me to my job. The bus did not come. So I started to walk to the next bus stop hoping to catch the next bus, so I waited there. I heard some kind of running noise of engines, army vehicles, tanks. I saw people running out of their houses, so I came back to my house. I sat -- as soon as I came, my wife said: "Why did you come back?" But I said: "No, I cannot go because the tanks and army vehicles are moving in our direction." So I had my breakfast and had a cup of coffee. I did not smoke for an hour or two. Then I saw three soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise who those soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came towards my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they called me. I came out of the house. Then they pointed their automatic guns, one had a machine gun, heavy machine gun, pointed at me and they asked me for weapons. I said: "I have no weapons".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these men dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two of them were dressed in the normal -- in the normal uniforms of the former army and one was in a mor colourful uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the former army, you are referring to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what the more colourful uniform represented at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know. It was just different. I saw it for the first time, I must say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what did they do when they came to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they asked me for weapons. I told them: "I have no weapons. I have just returned from work. I have no weapons".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they conduct a search of either you or your property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They did not enter my house. They looked around the house a little. But they separated me from my wife and children immediately, and they told me to go to my father who already had his hands at his back, behind his head, and as soon as I saw this I realised that they might want to kill me, but my wife and children actually remained there and I was -- I went to my father's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was your father's house in relation to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a little below my house, maybe 30, 20 to 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of village where your house was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Piskavica and Pustosi. There are two names for the same location, Piskavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is that from the city of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to this time, this is 2nd June 1992, had there been a change of administration in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some houses had been burnt. When I went t work or returned from work, I could see tanks and armoured vehicles at the point of entry into the town of Vlasenica. We were checked at the checking point and whenever I went, actually there was a guard with me so I would not escape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is when you went to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to have any papers to permit to you travel from your home in Piskavica to your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they asked -- we had the so-called passes. We were given these so that we could go to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long had you been going to work, approximately, for how long had you had to use these passes to go to and from your work to your home up until 2nd June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, as far as I can recall, around the 21st April, that was the time when it was introduced. Then until I was actually imprisoned, I think this was the time when we needed these passes, until the occupation of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I interrupted you. I would like to take you back to the point when you were told to go to your father's house. What happened at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to my father's house. I also had to have my hands behind my head. Then my wife and the three children were brought down and were then taken to another village. They asked me, sorry, the army people went -- the soldiers went to another village. They asked me if there were any villages on the same road. I said: "Yes". Two of them left and one soldier remained with us. The soldier allowed me then to smoke a cigarette -- I asked him -- and he actually, I could then take my hands down from m back. Then this was a bit of a rest for me. But in about an hour's time the other two soldiers returned, bringing with them a woman and an elderly man, I mean, both the couple were elderly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When these soldiers returned what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they took us some 500 metres from the house, asked us again to put our hands behind our heads, and my father and myself were the only men plus a man from another village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the other man's name from the other village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man that they brought with them, I used to know his name. I think Ibro Zekic and his wife, Zada. These are the only names that I remember. So we walked for about 500 metres with our hands behind our heads. That was the three men plus wives and children behind us. The guns were pointed at us so that we do not try to escape, and when I looked around there were more women and more men in front of a house. This was a Serb house. Then I felt a bit better because I saw people around. So they brought us all together. We stood there for three to four hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you standing for three to four hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were standing in the courtyard, in a yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was in the village of Piskavica, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that three to four hours, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there came two military trucks. They stopped and they put us all, some 50 people, on to these trucks. Then the people started screaming. Women were crying. Children were screaming. Then they said: "No, do not worry, do not worry, the men will come behind you" so the put us men also on the trucks, and we drove towards Vlasenica and I saw the situation. I saw some dead people along the road, and as we came closer to Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of these dead people that you saw on the road, did you recognise any of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised four men. I could only recognise those four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of these four men, do you know what religion they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of them involved in the army or military? Were they in active service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. They were civilians. They were all in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then where did you go when you went towards Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they brought us into town. They took us to the Bauxite company administrative building. Then two soldiers remained with us. They were guarding the truck and they started some negotiation. We did not stay long there, just about half an hour, and then we started again towards Pale. They said we go in the direction of Pale. Then we went to about -- for about 500 metres and then we turned, and they went towards the part of the town where my company was, where my work post was. So I said: "Well, we are now moving towards the dark 'mracni do dor' that is, the dark gorge, and I feared that you will be killed there". So I felt at one point that we stopped. I stopped mere the military sheds. They asked us to get off the trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were these military sheds? What was the name of the place where these military sheds were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Susica was the same

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said I think a moment ago that your company had property in this area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they called this "sheds".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your work were you familiar with this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I knew it very well. I knew this was a military installation, so we would always come there. I would be passing these sheds and there were always guards posted and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the camp I think you said you had to disembark off the trucks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the court what happened then after you got off the trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There we got off the truck and they started searching us. They took everything away. They seized everything we owned and they did not allow us to take anything in, the cigarettes, they left some cigarettes for me, and they took away my money, about 6 billion dinars of that kind of money from that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were searched. Do you know who searched you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not tell you right now because I was really in panic at the time, and so I cannot remember their names at this point, who did the search.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were dressed in the uniform of the former Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all the people that carried out the search dressed in this way

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who searched me had that uniform on. Some of them had these colourful camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone when you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only recognised the guard called Jovic and Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person Nikolic, did you know his full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he was called Nikolic, and also they called him "Jenki". That is how they called him around there. I cannot remember his surname now -- his name, only as Dragan Nikolic, and he was called "Jenki" around the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you known this person, Dragan Nikolic, before you arrived and saw him there that day at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had. He was a fellow student in the same class with me. He was a class mate. In the third and fourth form he was my class mate. And I used to see a lot of him in Vlasenica, but I did not socialise with him. I did not go to coffee houses with him. We did not spend time together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But during the period of your life leading up until 1992 is it fair to say that you saw him from time to time in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know then or did you subsequently discover what position this person, Dragan Nikolic, had in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as I arrived there I found out that he was some kind of commander of the camp, that he would be commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you after you were searched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After they searched me they took me to the hangar where I saw about 10 or even 20 people. They had just brough me there. By the end of the day about 100 people had been brought to the hangar and then some women were brought in too. They practically packed the hangar full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this person, Dragan Nikolic, say anything to the people when you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did say things. "I brought you" -- "Alija has made you come to this; he betrayed you", "Alija" meaning Alija Izetbegovic no doubt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That first night nothing happened. When women and children had gone, about 200 men remained behind, and then they started beating us. Dragan hit individual men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion Dragan took me out. He called my name, he took me out. There were two soldiers whom I did not recognise in camouflage uniforms. He said: "Here, young men, here is your supper tonight."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you beaten? With what were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was kicked and with -- I was hit with rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Sorry, I would like to ask the witness what does this mean, "You will have something to eat tonight, you will get something tonight, here is your supper"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that I should be beaten. That is what he meant. That is how I interpreted that. There was nothing else to interpret it. There was no other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was beaten on the back. I felt the rifle butt in my back and also they kicked me on my stomach, on the ribs, and when I fell down, when I -- then they started walkin over me. I cannot remember any of the details, any more details. I was just brought into the hangar after that. I lay down next to my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain conscious throughout the beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not remain conscious all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become unconscious and then regain consciousness again from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I regained consciousness on one occasion when they were beating me. I cannot claim how long it lasted, five, 10 or 20 minutes -- I think about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said you were brought back into the hangar after the beating were you able to walk at all on your own at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it take before you were able to walk on your own again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About seven days it took me to get well again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of this beating where was Dragan Nikolic, so far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic at the time, he had left. He did not hit me at that time. He went to the sentry post where their office was, the guards' office was. I could not see him. I could not see whether he came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the sentry post contained in the camp itself that Dragan Nikolic went to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the place where Dragan Nikolic used to go on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were about 20 metres from where we were

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Excuse me. I am sorry to interrupt, could we give the witness the plan which you showed us before about the camp in Susica to see whether he recognises it, and also to tell us where precisely Dragan Nikolic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was about to do that, your Honour. (Handed) Perhaps Mr. Dixon might help, perhaps the witness might be given a pen? (To the witness): Mr. Cakisic, would you please look at that map, the plan, that you see there. Firstly, do you recognise what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the camp for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the camp at Susica, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. Just looking at that camp, can you tell us, firstly, where the building is that you were retained in, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this upper one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. When you said that Dragan Nikolic went off at the time of your beating, can you show the place to which he went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He when to this guard house here, to this sentry post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the place where Dragan Nikolic normally stayed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did your beating take place, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just hold your pen on it for a moment longer? OK. Do you see in the plan immediately in front of you the power pole, the A frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see things happen at that particular place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were mostly tied to that tower and they were beaten there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the other black building, the one next to the one that you were stationed in, what was that building used for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That building had been used as a military facility. They came and took military uniforms from that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see behind the building in which you were kept, the hangar in which you were kept, two small little buildings? Perhaps you might point to them with your pen, if you can see what I am talking about. No, the other two buildings immediately behind. Yes, those two. Do you know what those buildings represent? No, the two little ones you originally had your pen on. That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. The other building which is the other small building by the fence, close by the fence, towards the back of the camp, would you put your pen on that one? Do you know what that building was used for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was our toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] A small point: I understood that it was the place where the guards were stationed. Could you specify, could you give us more details about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does your Honour want me to do that now?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Very quickly. Is it the toilets or is it where the guards were stationed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will ask the question. (To the witness): Jus looking at that plan again, can you tell us where the guards were stationed, the guard house? Would you point that out again for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was this shed and this was, as far as I remember, the toilet, the other one, and the one in front was the guard house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Point to the guard house again, please, just so we can see it and leave your pen there for the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you. Fine. Thank you very much. We will adjourn and resume again at 2.30. (Luncheon adjournment) 2.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Counsel for the Prosecution, before we resume the hearing of the testimony of Mr. Cakisic, I would like to ask you whether in your office, in your department, you have a photograph of Dragan Nikolic. If there is such a photo in existence, could it be made available to the witness and then, of course, naturally to the Tribunal as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a photograph but it is a very bad quality photograph. So we are reluctant to use it because it is such poor quality. Mr. Cakisic, when were you in the Susica camp, did you know three detainees there, by the names of Muharem Kolarevic, a Mr. Zekic and Mr. Dzevad Saric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I used to know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What religion were these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they of military background or civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were civilians

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is that you know of these three men when you were in that camp at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I knew they were people just as I was a person, that they had been taken from their homes like myself, and I knew them as good people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to them that you saw when you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first I saw Dzevad Saric when he was taken out. The guard came by the name of Jovic. He took Dzevad out of the hangar around midnight or maybe 11 o'clock or midnight as far as I can remember. He was beaten. I heard his wailing and screaming and crying because while he was being beaten. Around 2 o'clock in the morning, at 2 o'clock after midnight, I heard a burst of gunfire, and then the guard, the same guard, entered the room. He took Muharem Kolarevic and Muso Zekic, I think he was Nusret Zekic in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They also a man from Kalesija. Then after two or three minutes we heard two bursts of fire and these people never came back or never appeared in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That night when those events were happening, did you see anyone in the camp other than the guard that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was also Dragan Nikolic who was present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you saw Dragan Nikolic and what he was doing when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was in the guard house. I think that everything was done according to his orders, and actually the guard took these people and that they beat these people especially Dzevad Saric; he suffered greatly and was tortured from what I heard, from what I heard from his wailing, but I assumed that it was all done according to the rule, orders given by Nikolic, as only three people were taken out also according to his orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw Nikolic that night these men were taken out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day were you asked to do something in relation to these three men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The following morning around 4 o'clock they ordered me and one other person, two more persons, so the three of us came out, four perhaps I am sorry, I cannot remember exactly, so we were asked to collect these bodies. The bodies, they were in a ditch between the guard house and the hangar. It had been raining, so there was some water in the ditch, some 10 centimetres in the ditch. So we collected them. We then took them towards Zalokavlje, towards the Mracni Do, gorge. We buried them there. One guard also wanted to kill us, not to have any witnesses, not to have any surviving witnesses, but then another man, a Serb, I do not know him, he said: "Don't touch these people", and so we were not killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see what sort of condition the bodies were in when you collected them from the ditch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were bullet ridden from bursts of fire and from rifle fire. Dzevad was also beaten, you could see that, also cut with the knife. That is as far as I could see and assess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea about when this event occurred i times of date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This happened around the 25th or 26th. The dates I think are correct. I am fairly confident that that was one of these dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also while you were at this camp at Susica, did you know of a person who was known by the name of Durmo and a man called Asim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him. Asim I knew. I also knew Durmo by sight. I used to meet him in Vlasenica in our town, so I knew him I may say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of something that happened to them while you were at the Susica camp that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. On 15th, between the 15th and 20th June around 11 o'clock, 12 o'clock in the evening the two of them were taken out. I think Dragan Nikolic was also present. They beat them and the two men started

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: crying, suffering from great pain, calling for help, so they were beaten until maybe half past 1 or 2 o'clock

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: after midnight. Then Asim was brought into the hangar again and Durmo after him. They were actually carried into the hangar and Asim could not stand on his feet. They had been beaten so badly and the other detainees

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: helped them, placing them on their, in their places where they were lying. Asim was almost was half dead. Then in about an hour's time he was really dead; he was such a broken and bruised man. In the meantime he sometimes regained consciousness and then fainted again. Durmo suffered such great pain that he could not sleep. Then Dragan Nikolic came the following morning. Durmo asked us to give him a pill against pain, but Draga Nikolic came around 8 or 9 o'clock the following morning. We covered Durmo because he was shivering and he was all swollen. Dragan Nikolic came to him and he removed the

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: blanket and said, "Who is this?" We said, "This is Durmo". He say: "Uncover him. He doesn't need to be

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: covered so that he suffers and dies." Durmo then got up, asked Dragan, said, "Dragan, please kill me", and Dragan then answered: "Durmo, you must first suffer greatly and then die. The bullet costs German mark and you are not worth a cigarette butt." So Durmo again started pleading with him and said, "Dragan, please kill me." Dragan was on his way towards the door, he made three to four steps. Durmo walked, crawled after him. Again he said: "Dragan, please", he asked Dragan to kill him. He again said: "No, no, you must suffer, you most tell me where your sons are." Durmo says: "I have no idea. I don't know." So Dragan made one more step towards the door, most probably, and at that time Durmo died on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in your evidence that when you arrived at the camp, first arrived at the camp, they took away from you the money that you had in your possession which is, I think you said, 6 billion dinar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that took this money from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the man precisely. No, no. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what the 6 billion dinar would have been in, say, deutschemarks approximately, roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. It might have been on the average, I do not remember the exchange rate at that moment

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just your best estimate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 600 marks maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain, describe for their Honours the conditions that existed in the camp and the conditions that you experienced at the Susica camp when you were there in terms of the hygiene, toilets and the accommodations generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was fairly horrible. We slept on the concrete floor. Even Dragan did not allow people to bring a board, a wooden board. They said: "Let them sleep on the concrete floor, that would be better for them than on a couch." So we had to sleep like this. We had a jacket, somebody had a coat, so we rolled this and then slept as best we could and sat on it later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the food? What was the food that you were given like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received food, a piece of bread every day for 24 hours, then one ladle full of boiled potatoes, maybe boiled beans or whatever was brought. That was all for the full 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One piece of bread?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just an ordinary sized bowl, how big was the bowl, big or small bowl?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a small portion. How can I say? This size, for instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the hygiene, were you able to shower or bath while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No, we were not even allowed to go out and wash our feet. It was difficult even to obtain a permit to g to the toilet. They brought some pails, some buckets into which we had to urinate, even defecate. There was no bath, nothing. I could not wash my feet and what else could I have done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The toilet you had to urinate in and defecate in, was there any screen or privacy provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. This was behind the door of the hangar. Everybody could see and they saw everything of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Excuse me, on this particular point, the question of hygiene and sharing your life together, what about the women, were they subjected to the same conditions or were they separated? What about the hygiene for them, the physiological and food needs of, I think it was, eight women in the camp? Could you the tell us further details about that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] No, they were bound to do it in the same bucket, men and women, everybody in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about clothes, were you permitted to change your clothes at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No, we had nothing to change. There was nothing to change into.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at Susica camp were you required at any stage to do duties outside of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken people, were taken to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What work were you taken to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was collecting bodies, dead bodies along the road, then also in the village on Jamici and Gradinia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The dead bodies that you collected along the road, do you know were these bodies dressed in civilian clothes or i military clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all this civilian clothes merely solely in civilian clothes. Some of them were in their pyjamas even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bodies that you collected, were they all male or male and female? Were they adults? Were they children, old people? Can you tell us the mix of the people that you picked up to bury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were men, all of them were men, let us say between the ages of 40 and 50 I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate while you were doing this duty approximately how many bodies you had to collect and take and bury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that in all three villages altogether I collected about 100 dead bodies, and buried them of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the bodies that you collected from outside of the Susica camp, and apart from the people that you have already mentioned about burying, did you ever have to bury any other bodies from the camp at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, you are asking whether people from the Susica camp that were killed, they were also collected?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you collect any other bodies apart from the bodies of Muharem Kolarevic, Zekic and Dzevad Saric who you have already told the court about, did you bury any other bodies from the Susica camp during the period of time that you were staying there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You see, Kolarevic, Halil and Savco Jamjic, then Durmo. I am not sure about one of the names. There was a man whose name I do not recall

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you bury these bodies? Did you bury them all in the one place or did you bury them in different places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at Mracni Do, that was the dredgers came and they made holes and we put bodies into the holes, and they piled earth on top of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these dredgers, as you call them, designed to dig up the ground? They were mechanical machines for digging up the ground, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were mechanical machines for digging. Yes, that is exactly what they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they always at this place or did they only ever come there when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came from time to time and then left and came again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at this place, did you only ever see the graves that you put bodies into or did you see other mounds around the place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were the people that, we buried these people into these holes, while the four people that I first mentioned were buried separately, Muharem, Kolarevic, Musa and the Kalesija man whose name I do not remember, they were buried separately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay when you were held in the camp at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 26 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened, can you describe to the Tribunal the circumstances of how it was that you came to leave Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember clearly the 28th June. They came, Dragan Nikolic, to call our names to go and be exchanged. He called our names and we went out one by one. While w were going out and going towards the bus there was a distance of about 30 or 40 metres to cover from the hangar to the bus where we were collected. There were men in camouflage uniform on both sides. As we came out of the hangar we were hit and kicked; as we approached one of those each one kicked us and hit us. "That is what you get for voting for Alija. Now you are going to be exchanged. You can go." When I went into the bus I was hit with a rifle butt. I sat down. I did not know what was going on. I did not even rest, "Why don't you put down your head in the bus?" I did not know these men personally but I know they had come from Sekovici. They were wearing some hats, not even cowboys had such hats. There were three buses, bus loads of people and we headed in an unknown direction. I do not know where I was going. We went, we drove for about three or four hours, and they brought us to the Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Batkovic camp what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I experienced there a real catastrophe. They took us out of the bus, bus by bus, and they crammed us into corners and kept hitting us. They also searched us again and took us into the hangar. When they finished one group they made us crawl along the hangar, on the floor of the hangar, and kept hitting us. That was really horrible. I thought to myself, I could not take this for more than 24 hours, but I endured all that crawling on the concrete. There was a lot of dust around. They would not let us take anything in, anything that we can sleep on. I know when we came they gave us some food. We had supper there the following morning. They started beating u again. They kept coming in and beating us. When we came in a machine gun, 53 millimetres, was positioned and also there was a guard there with the machine gun: "If anybody moves you'll all be killed." The second day they brought more people, three or four bus loads of people. We were ordered to lie down on our stomach, so that we could not see who came and who were the escorts. They kept asking us for money and for gold objects. We said, "No, you have taken everything away." One day a man came with a whistle with a hat on. He kept beating them and they kept giving him things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you stay in Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fourteen and a half months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Batkovic camp where then did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of what you have suffered, have you any continuing condition or pain as a result of what happened to you, both in the camp at Susica and at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As time goes by I feel pain in my back, my kidneys and in my crotch. Whenever the weather changes, especially a sudden change of weather, I feel that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you. I look at my two colleagues. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you. Mr. Cakisic, you told us that in Susica camp your father was there, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Yes, my father was brought to the same camp with me. He came about on about 27th June. He was to be exchanged and taken to Kladanj to be exchanged. There were also women and children and old men. They took the to Srpske. He was alive until Srebrenica fell to Serbs, and then after that all traces of him are lost. He is missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your father and other older people, as well as women and children were there, all of them were beaten and suffered the same conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a lot of beating. Dragan Nikolic in particular asked a woman, an 85 year old woman, to marry him. He said he will rape you, he pointed to a man and said, "He will rape you", there was a lot of that kind of talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he rape the woman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Not in front of us. He did take them out and mistreated them, but I did not see that, he did not do it in front of us. He brought the guards, "Would you like to marry", and would ask the women, "Would you like to marry this guard or that guard?" There was a lot of questions like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In front of you and the other inmates of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not see anything of that, any of the action. I just saw heard these questions. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to ask was there any common feature between all those whom you saw executed or dead? Were they in the resistance, in some kind of resistance or did they pick them just at random without any reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were randomly picked. They were taken out of their houses. As far as I know they did not take part in any military group or army or they did not have any weapons either. This is at least my opinion, and becaus I know these people quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave the order of the killing? Was it Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Nikolic was the one who gave the orders. He was the one who decided on everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in the name of the JNA or in the local military or local police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was all done on behalf of the SDS party, the Serbian, so-called Serbian Democratic Party. He was chosen as the main commander because everything was done as he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this Serbian democratic party related to Belgrade or was it a local party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think everything was linked to Belgrade. When Vlasenica was occupied the people who came in tanks and armoured vehicles, they were from Novi Sad, I spoke to these people. I had some contact with them when I passed them by, when they checked my documents, and I found out they were from Novi Sad, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave the order, who gave you the order to do the burying direct? Was it Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nikolic was the one who ordered us to do the burying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Cakisic, as regards the daily management of the camp in Susica, we have the impression that the guards did not really foresee any daily management. Was there a time that you had to get up go to sleep? Was there a time for leaving the hangar, even if it be for one hour, so that could you walk in the yard? You stayed there for one month. Did you have the -- when I listen to you it seems to me that thing happened at random, you came without any clothing, you slept on cement, whereas there was a commander of the camp, but there does not seem to be any internal rules. You can also talk about the next camp if you stayed there longer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that at Susica we were not allowed to walk out. I personally asked Dragan Nikolic to let me out. I was once forced out in my rubber boots because I had boils on my feet from the sweat. He would not even let us take off these boots. You had to wear the boots all the time. I just wanted to wash my feet, but he would not let us do that. We could not go out of the hangar. "You don't need to wash; you will not live much longer anyhow." We had to ask for everything. In the morning we were not woken up by anybody. Then about 10 people were taken out to go to the toilet about 12 o'clock in the evening and that was about the only time when we were allowed out. We could not even go out to have a drink of water. It was the same thing in Batkovic. For three months I did not go out; they would not let us. Then when they put the barbed wire fence around the hangar for three months we did not go out. We urinated in the hangar in barrels and metal barrels which were cut into half. This is where we urinated and defecated for three months until we were registered by the Red Cross. When we were registered by the Red Cross then they would let us out. They made a toilet outside. Then we went out and they beat us less after that time too. Those who had been beaten were not allowed to say anything or to complain to the Red Cross because the following day he would disappear and he woul be beaten up completely. One day they sent me to forced labour -- I was registered by the Red Cross and they sent me to a place where we had to do forced labour. I will never forget that day. There were 40 people of us; there were 40 of us. They were given a slice of bread and an egg; we were given a slice of bread and an egg. They put us in a bus: "You have to go to work" we were told. We were driven for about an hour and a half. When we came to the work site I saw some weapons that I had never seen before, three barrels. They chased us out of the bus, gave us some spades. They gave access to some inmates, one had a power saw. They told him to clean the area 50 metres on each side of the road. While we were working there praying to God to be killed if I had to work another day, I thought I would rather be dead, I would rather be dead. They sent you about 50 metres away from the asphalt road to work. There is a guard that I remember. They would take me along the road and they would call our names. He had a truncheon about this size, a wooden bat about this thick. He would call you to come to the asphalt part of the road, "Turn your back to me", he would say. I did so. He would hit you three times and then you have to run back to your job. You go there and then they would call you again and then when you come there they would say, "Why didn't you run?" and I ran as fast as I could. Often I had only had a slice of bread and an egg before that. Then you come up there and then they hit you again at least three times whenever you came to him. That is how it went on I endured one day like that. Then lunch time came about 3 o'clock in the afternoon, a slice of bread with some liver paste on it. I could not even eat. I could not work. My hands were bloody. I took that slice of bread to eat it. Then again the guards called me because there were some bushes to be taken care of, and I prayed to God and they told me to go down and then they would take away the tools from my hands and told me to use my hands and dig the earth with my hands. Also I had to sing some Chetnik songs at the same time. I did not know how to sing, how to sing these because I had never heard these songs before, and he forced me to sing songs that I did not know. When we got on the bus on our way back to go to Batkovic, the guard called whose name was Zoran or nickname Zoka, he was there. They drank beer. They would have a crate of beer and drink. As we were entering the camp and the commander was there, Drago, he asked in front of him: "Did you have a good time, boys? Are you going to go there tomorrow again?" I had to say: "Yes, it was good" and I could barely walk, stand on my feet. My back was all bruised up. If I had lived that day I thought to myself I would live a long time after that. I was not allowed to complain to the Red Cross because I knew I would be put to even worse torture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point of time in the first camp or the second camp was there an attempt to revolt in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no opportunity to rebel in any sense at all. We all felt that we were honest men, that we had not killed anybody. We had not done anything wrong to any o these people. They simply put me and my neighbours, put me to prison, detained for 13 and a half months without any normal living conditions. The Red Cross came to our salvation, I must say, because it guaranteed some security. Also every fortnight we would get meat tins and some other food, otherwise we would have died. We had no vitamins, nothing. We had food that was neither fat nor salt; had no salt. We actually complained but they said, "Well, eat that." I do not eat anything better, but what was there was just boiled water and three beans and three pieces of potato perhaps. We complained to the Red Cross. The Red Cross said: "Well, but we are giving food for you", but that food got lost between the donors and us.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Your testimony has now reached its conclusion. I would like you to understand that you are in front of the International Criminal Tribunal. Before you leave do you want to add anything? Do you wish to say something, perhaps something that we have not covered when we asked you questions through the Prosecutor or the questions put by the Judge? Do you wish to add something? If you do, please, this is the moment to do so, otherwise your testimony is finished now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] I would have nothing at the moment that I would like to add. I know that I am here at the International Tribunal. I feel no guilt. I spoke the truth. I only described what I saw and what I lived through and I have no reason to be ashamed of what I have done here or elsewhere. I speak openly and frankly, and have nothing else to add

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you. The Tribunal would like to thank you for your testimony. If you could now accompany the witness and then have the next witness come forward. Please accompany this witness out and bring the next witness to the stand. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may ask ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] I have one question from Judge Riad. Is Mr. Gow still in The Hague, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: I will defer to Mr. Niemann who I believe knows much more about Mr. Gow's schedule than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I understand he is still here in The Hague. He was at least at lunch-time anyway, so I assume he is still here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] The Tribunal would like to ask him one or two supplementary questions after his testimony yesterday. Would it be possible either this afternoon or tomorrow at an agreed time that Dr. Gow could come forward again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand Dr. Gow is going back tonight, so if you have some more questions it would be most convenient if we could do it almost immediately. I will make some enquiries to see if we can bring him down here. Would your Honour excuse me so I can go and see where he is? My colleague will take over.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. If I could be excused to make sure that the next witness does not have any security concerns? There was some question about that and before calling him I would like to double check.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Yes

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Somebody might make those enquiries for us about Dr. Gow, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to the next witness, I have doubled checked with him. He does wish to testify publicly, so I would ask that your Honours lift the protective order with respect to this witness other than his address.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Will the Court Clerk and will the Registrar take note of this request, and make sure that it is listed that the Tribunal has acceded to this. We will not reveal the identity of the next witness but all other elements, except the address -- sorry, we will not reveal the address. However, the next witness will be named.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution will call Mr. Amir Berbic. Amir Berbic, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Amir Berbic, first of all can you hear everything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Amir Berbic, first of all you will read the oath which you have before you in your language of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Be seated. Mr. Berbic, we are very grateful that you have come here. We know that the travelling conditions were difficult, so thank you very much. You are before an International Criminal Tribunal, so within a legal framework and, therefore, you also have legal protection. Therefore, you can give your testimony in all security and safety If at any point you find it very difficult to continue, please let us know. Counsel for the Prosecution, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Amir Berbic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 24th April 1962, so I am 33 years old now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war how were you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked at the factory of aluminium and castings and I was a machine tool operator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of that company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A factory for the production of aluminium castings Alpro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened in Vlasenica in the later part of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April that year -- would you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask that you may be moved closer to the microphones a little bit? May I ask you move closer to the microphones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, with my apologies to Mr. Berbic, Mr. Niemann has given me a note that Mr. Gow is here now and scheduled to leave as soon as possible, so if your Honours want to hear from Mr. Gow again, with my apologies to Mr. Berbic, I suggest maybe we interrupt this if your Honours want to hear from Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] What time does Mr. Gow have to leave at, please?

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: He has an appointment somewhere else I believe not associated with his work here, at 4 o'clock in Holland. Then he is scheduled to fly home immediately after his 4 o'clock appointment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Fine. Well, Mr. Berbic, the Tribunal would like to apologise to you. We do have to take a few 1 minutes, just a few minutes to listen once again to a witness whom we had here yesterday. So we would like you to go back to the room where you were for a few minutes. There are just a couple of questions for this witness and during that time of course we would like you to remain available to the Tribunal, I think it will only last about 10 or 15 minutes, before we ask you to come back again. Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Would you like to show Dr. Gow in? Dr. James Gow, Recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Please sit down. Dr. Gow, the Tribunal on the part of one of its members, would like a few more details from you, please, and therefore I would like to give the floor to Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you for coming back, Mr. Gow. Going through your yesterday's testimony I gathered, as well as my colleagues, that you implied that Belgrade was directly involved in the conflict in Bosnia. I have not even to ask you questions about it. You mentioned giving forces in Bosnia, giving the Serbs in Bosnia newer Defence systems, co-ordinating attacks, giving piece of equipment, a newer Defence system and so on. This very important information deserves substantiation. Would you be able to give us your sources, the sources for which we can hav confirmation of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I have understood the question correctly, then I can say that the information that I gave you is based on reports that have been made in public places, reports of different kinds, some in press, some in documents provided in what I suppose could be described as officials places and on discussions with people who either were able to witness certain things, or who are familiar with what was going on in particular situations as a result of either being involved or talking to people who were involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are some of these documents at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of the materials I described are not at my immediate disposal, but they are at my disposal generally and I can point you to them or with the assistance of the Office of the Prosecutor can provide you with some of the material I described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That would be very important. Thank you very much. That is all.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Counsel for the Prosecution, do you have an additional question for Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I do not have an additional question, your Honour, but I think that it may take some time to extract the necessary documentation and make it available. I would need to confer with Dr. Gow. There is some material held in the Office of the Prosecutor now that has been prepared in another matter, but I am not sure whether it forms part of that material or not. I would need to enquire. I do not think that I could do it at least until I had an opportunity to confer with Dr. Gow over the afternoon adjournment

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Yes. I am maybe reading my colleague's mind here, but were you referring to documents which you would like to get hold of straightaway?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But it is important to have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, well, if I have them would your Honours accept them being handed up from the bar table by the Prosecution or would you require Dr. Gow to give the documents? I only say that because of his arrangements regarding returning to England. I understand he is going back to England tonight.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] No. Dr. Gow is, of course, going to go home this evening. Let me reassure him of that straightaway. What is the context of this request? Well, it is part of our procedures. We are dealing with Article 61. It is not, as such, the trial of Dragan Nikolic; it is just a confirmation of the indictment. This is the context of sufficient and reasonable presumption. However, Dr. Gow was brought by you to the Tribunal. We will have to see if Judge Riad agrees with this, but I think that this complementary information, if the Tribunal confirms the indictment following this hearing, then at that point in time we will continue our investigations and at that particular point it would then be up to the Prosecution to meet the needs of the Tribunal and at that point obtain documents from Dr. Gow which Dr. Gow has just referred to. Would that suit you, Counsel for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. It is just that I needed time. I could not do it straightaway. So long as we have time to make it available that should be fine

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] The floor is yours, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] If I may be permitted one small point to correct something that I said yesterday. I am aware that in part of my answer to your Honour Judge Riad at the end of yesterday when you asked me about specific dates, I believe I said that the action to divide the JNA was on 22th May. When I noted what I said I realised it was a mistake and it should have been 19th May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you very much. Do we have further questions of Dr. Gow from either the Office of the Prosecutor or the bench, the other Judges? I do not think any of us have any further questions. So, once again, Dr. Gow, thank you very much for having come so quickly once again to the Tribunal. Once again also thank you for your testimony from yesterday. We would like to wish you a good journey back to the rest of your activities. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Kindly show Mr. Berbic in. Mr. Amir Berbic, Recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
