utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Berbic, please sit down. At the point when we broke off Miss McHenry did in fact ask a question. I believe that the witness had not fully understood or heard the question. So maybe you could rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, was there anything significant that happened in Vlasenica with respect to who controlled the town or who administered the town that occurred in lat April 1992? Mr. Berbic, are you hearing my questions? I think maybe it is on a different channel.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Could somebody help Mr. Berbic to find the correct channel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Now it is all right. Do you understand Mr. Berbic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Miss McHenry, would you please repeat the question in order to make sure that the witness fully understands it.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, did anything happen in Vlasenica in late April 1992 with respect to a change in the running of the administration of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, let me try to explain. Vlasenica was occupied on 21st April 1992. Many things changed. Let me say that the Bosnian people, especially the Bosniacs, went through many traumas. Many people started fleeing away, people were hiding, those that could hide; those that could flee fled, so it was possible to flee and reach the free territory. While during the occupation nobody could actually leave Vlasenica, many people were killed trying to escape, and then came that fateful moment when we were taken to the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get to that part, Mr. Berbic, may I ask you who occupied Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vlasenica was occupied by the Serbian and Montenegro aggressors. I talked to them, to some of them, and I learned they were from the Novi Sad Corps they were people mostly Serbs from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you talked to them, what did the people, the soldiers you talked to, tell you

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we talked to them and they told me that they came to calm down the situation, although there was no unrest, there was nothing, and then we realised that in broad daylight the Bosnian Serbs started arming each other, each was passing weapons to the other. So this created a lot of fear and it was impossible for us to go on living like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how long the Novi Sad soldiers stayed in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they stayed approximately for a month or month and a half, at least that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both during the time, prior to the occupation and then during the occupation prior to your arrest, were you involved in any sort of military groups or any armed resistance to the occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all, not at all, because people, few people had any weapons at all. Nobody was prepared in any way, people were not armed. The only people who had arms were perhaps in other towns and villages like Cerska and they did offer some resistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred a moment ago to the day you were brought to Susica. Can you tell us what day that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was on 2nd June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were sitting at home. It was me, my father, my brother, and around 9 or 10 o'clock in the morning the door was actually open, and then suddenly we saw in our door two soldiers armed with semi-automatic guns and also hand grenades, two hand grenades, hanging from their belts. They surprised us and since I knew both of thes people, one was Milomir Janjusevic and the other was Ostoja Radic. So they collected the three of us and we also collected on our way Huso Jusic, that was our neighbour, and we were taken towards the camp. I asked, "Where are you taking us?" and they said: "For an interview."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we walked for 200 or 300 metres and then these two told soldiers handed us over to other two soldiers who I do not know, but they came, I know they came from their village called Cikote. They also had automatic rifles and hand grenades hanging on their belts, from their belts. So we walked. We came close to the camp, some 500 metres. They asked us to put our hands behind our heads, and we marched on. At one point the last person in the row, whose name I do not remember, stopped my brother and said, "Stop all of you." Now I just remembered, at that moment I thought they would kill us. We did not know what they wanted, but they took his wedding ring. So they took his wedding ring. They took my father's and my own watch, and after a minute or two we moved towards the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "camp" what camp are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Susica, the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at the Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived in the Susica camp we were ordered to let our hands down. Then we were searched. I had a packet of cigarettes. I had my lighter, cigarette lighter. They did not take it away from me. I met several guards there, but I had no idea what it was and why they were there. The search lasted for about five to six minutes. The they told us to enter the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So what happened was that from the hangar, I was in the hangar, a man by the man of name Garic, whose first name I do not know, called me to come out. He said, "Berbic, come out." So I came out. He started provoking me, me and my neighbour, Cane Reljic, and he said that Cane Reljic and he were in my house, that they found knives and needles, although I had no idea about that because I had nothing like that. So he started beating me. He spoke abusively of my mother. He had a machine gun. He hit me on the head. I had a cut on my forehead, also he beat me on the hands and the feet. This lasted for 20 minutes to half an hour. Then he ordered me to go back to the hangar, so I did that as I was told. Everybody standing on the side was laughing and watching while I was being beaten by Garic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say everyone who was standing around was watching and laughing, do you mean other prisoners or do you mean guards or who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean the detainees. No, no, sorry, very sorry, I mean the guards, of course I mean the guards. There were some eight to 10 guards surrounding us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you were allowed to return to the hangar? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I entered the hangar and I saw some 200 to 300 people, including women, children, elderly people, younger people. They were all lined up, some of them asked why they were there. Nobody understood anything, nobody knew anything. So everybody started questioning everybod else. An hour later they asked more, the guards asked questions such as do we know of anybody who had any weapons. I said I did not know anybody who had any weapons. Ilic's was a man, a guard, who called me every hour or two hours. He mistreated me, beat me, and there were three or four other people whose names I do not know, they call came from Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said he called you every hour or so, do you mean during that first stay you were brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe I should say on that day this was once or twice, but then the whole procedure was repeated for the following five to six days while we were still in the camp. I know Ilic very well and I know his father, but I do not remember his first name. He had a scar and he had been in Croatia in Vukovar the Vukovar offensive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The subsequent beatings that occurred for the next five to six days, were they similar to the beatings that you told us about on the first day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was similar. I was kicked. I was hit with rifle butts, and I had pains in my kidneys, so I felt some consequences of the beatings. I noticed I also had a scar above my upper lip. I had a cut lip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Dragan Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Dragan very well and I have known him for more than -- almost 20 years. He worked in the same company, Alpro in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him at Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time when we were first brought, during the first few days, he was not there. I know only when he did come he actually brought with him some 230 to 250 people detainees, mostly from villages of Kalesije, Cerska and other villages. These were the elderly people, younger people, some minors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those detainees join you and the other approximately I believe you said 300 detainees who were already at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These detainees were arriving day by day and they were all from the neighbouring villages, women and children and so on, people who had been hiding in the forest, and as soon as they people arrived they placed them on the right side of the hangar. So practically one half of the hangar was filled with these people and again there was the concrete floor. They were asked to sit down, not to speak among themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the over 500 detainees all kept in the same hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were all kept in the same building. I forgot to mention that they were also brought from the secondary school not far from my house, and before that, before they were brought to the camp, they had been kept in the gymnasium of the secondary school for some two weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Dragan Nikolic's role at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan was the commander of the camp. He used to say to the prisoners as to be addressed as the Serbian soldier captain, commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever say anything else to the prisoners about his role and his position as opposed to the prisoners' role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to saying that he wished to be called captain, did Dragan Nikolic ever speak to the prisoners about hi role and his power over them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said: "I am God here, and I am the stick. God and the stick." That he had to be addressed as commander or captain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there was a detainee called Durmo Handzic at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know Durmo Handzic quite well. He had been a porter in the building, of the administration building of the Bauxite company. A man in his early 60s, tall, white haired. I know two of his sons too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a man named Asim Zildzic at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know Asim Zildzic too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Asim Zildzic, about how old he was, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. He was about 60 years old. He had worked in the furniture factory called the 10th August in Vlasenica. I know his wife, Rasema.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you see happen to Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that on about 21st or 22nd June before that time Dragan had maltreated them and had beaten them. He was called -- Durmo was called one day and Asim him too on about 21st or 22nd June at about between 10.00 and 12.00 in the evening they were called out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who called them out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the door opened and, judging by the voices that I heard, I recognised Pero, Pero Popovic, Goran Tesic and Dragan was there too, Dragan Nikolic was there too. They were told to go out and they did as they were commanded to

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever did you see any of those individuals, in particular, Dragan Nikolic or Goran Tesic or any of the other individuals you mentioned as Durmo and Asim were going out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, they ordered them to go out, and they had been standing by the door, about five or six metres from the door, and I saw Dragan carrying a wooden bat about a metre long, yes, and hit Durmo while Dragan kept kicking the other one, the other man, and they went to the left side, about five or six metres from that point to the post where there was the floodlight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recollect vaguely that, whether the door was closed or not, I heard screams and moans, especially as Dragan was hitting him and asking him where his sons were, where Durmo's sons were. Durmo kept saying he knew nothing about his sons. They had escaped earlier. I also heard the voice of Goran Tesic who said to Durmo -- who said to Asim, asking him where he had dug his weapons and whether he had any weapons. That may have lasted for about one hour, an hour and a half, that beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time was there any other detainee who was taken out for any part of that time besides Durmo and Asim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that I think there was another one or two inmates. They were also taken out that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if someone, Mirsad was taken out at all that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirsad Smajlovic, I think, was also taken out. He wa also taken out on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after the beating had been going on for about an hour or more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That beating continued and then Asim came back first. He was carried or, rather, dragged by Hasim Ferhatovic and his brother, Alija, and I think the Mirsad was there too. They were taken to their sleeping places. They laid him down on this place because he was beaten up badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he" do you mean Asim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Asim, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard moans. Then Durmo came after him, Durmo Handzic, who was in the corner of the hangar on the left side, at the far end of the hangar. Durmo was barely able to walk but he kept holding his stomach and he sobbed. I also heard the screams coming from Asim Zildzic. He sobbed. They had terrible pains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most people there in the hangar slept and then about 2.00 or 3 o'clock I heard that one of the inmates said that Durmo -- that Asim had died, while the other fellow was sleeping about five or six metres from me, Durmo Handzic. He was sleeping next to a neighbour of his, Mujo Maljisevic. He sobbed. Mujo kept sobbing. Durmo, he had very strong pains, intensive pains. Someone poured water over him. He was all swollen. All his left side was swollen. He was also dirty. We could see that quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly what time it was. When Dragan cam to the hangar he started to provoke the inmates. It seems to me that he did not know that Asim had died. He stood about five or six metres from Durmo and ordered other inmates not to help him or not to give him any water or any kind of help. "Let him suffer", he said, and that is what happened. The next morning, about 10 or 11 o'clock, Durmo Handzic staggered and came to the door and suddenly fell, collapsed, about two or three metres before the door. Dragan came up to him and provoked him, interrogated him. He put his foot on his chest and again asked him: "Where are your sons?" He again said he did not know anything about their whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told him he knew nothing about them. Dragan was a tall man. He put his foot on his chest. He provoked him. He wept, Durmo wept, and turned around, wiggled. He kept asking him where his sons were. He kept -- and Durmo kept asking him to kill him and Dragan said he was not worth a cigarette butt. He asked him again to kill him. He says: "No, you are not worth a bullet because a bullet is two deutschemarks and you are not worth that."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that provoking by Dragan, Durmo died after about an hour, and a lot of inmates were panicked. We really suffered a lot, saw all sorts of horrors, all the inmates there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Asim and Durmo's bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Asim's body was carried out the following morning by Hasim Ferhatovic and his brother Alija, nickname "Gico". The were carried out, I do not know exactly where, while Durmo's body was also taken out. I do not know what happened later and where they took him. I think they carried Durmo to a place behind the hangar in the direction of the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did witnessing this event that you have just described have any physical effect on you or have any psychological effect on you immediately after it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. It had an effect on me. It was hard to experience all that. I went through three camps and I was beaten in all the three camps, but I am fine still. I am OK.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to ask about something else now. Do you want me to go on or would you think this a convenient time to take the afternoon break?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] You can continue with one or two questions and we will have break in about five minutes time and then continue at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] As far as I am concerned, I can go on. It all depends on you. I can answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there a Dzevad Saric at the camp, a detainee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Dzevad was beaten by Dragan. Dzevad Saric, I know him. He is from a village. I cannot remember the name of the village. They were beaten during the day. Before those two died, Kolarevic, Muharem and also Asertin Sefko, he is from the area of Zvornik, they were beaten three or four days before those two were killed, they were beaten by Dragan and another guard called Reljic, Cane, hi nickname was Cane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether or not there was ever a time when Dzevad Saric and the other people you have mentioned, Muharem Kolarevic and another gentleman, were taken out and then did not return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that happened on the 22nd or 23rd June. After them -- one day after that they were taken out that evening. I cannot quite remember who took them out. But we could hear, five minutes after that we could hear, rounds of fire and individual shots in the vicinity, maybe in the immediate vicinity, maybe 10 or 15 metres from the hangar, on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] I suggest Mr. Berbic, counsel for the Prosecutor, that we now have a break for 15 minutes and resume again at 4.30. (Short Adjournment) (4.30 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Berbic, could you describe generally the conditions at Susica camp, including the food and sanitary hygiene facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I say that from the beginning, when we were first brought to the camp, the entire camp was just one building with a concrete floor, and we slept on it. Somebody might have had some kind of piece of cloth or an item of clothing, so the whole hangar was a concrete structure. As for food, after four or five days when we -- after we had been brought in, they started serving us one meal per day. That was -- and the food was very -- was stale food. There might have been one or two pieces of bread ver thinly cut, a slice of very thin. And when Dragan came, when we had to go to the toilet, there were usually up to 50 people brought and then they would give us a minute, not more than a minute, and the guards took us to the toilet and then we had to -- and were brought back. Everything you had to do there you had to do within a single minute. It was cold and the concrete was cold. The concrete floor was cold. I was swollen, my tooth -- I had a toothache, I had no pain killer. Because people who were there were from villages, people who had lived in the forest before for two to three months hiding there, so some of them got scabies. I had also felt itchy, and then we also get lice. Everybody had lice. There were no sanitary conditions. It might have been better if they had killed us from the start.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many guards were there at the camp, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were seven to eight guards stationed around in front of the building perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the acts of abuse that you have described this afternoon the only acts of abuse that occurred while you were at Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was -- there were beatings, I was beaten, then people from these villages were beaten. When I was beaten by Garic, I was beaten, I was beaten, he said, because I had done something 15 years earlier where I was a good soccer player, and then he remembered that because he played against me in a team against me and now he said: "Now you will pay for that." He seemed to remember these things. Even those who were killed were killed fo something which might have happened 10 to 20 years earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left Susica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, while the toilet was being built behind the hangar and they asked: "Who has nails, any nails?" and since I lived some 800 metres or 1 kilometre away, I said I had some nails at home, which I did. So a former policeman took me there in his car, took me to my house. I saw horror. Buildings were destroyed. Because my house was on the left-hand side of the road, and there were three houses there, mine, where I lived with my father and mother, and then my brothers, my two brothers' houses, they were totally demolished. When I entered my house, because my father my father was a hunter and we had two dogs, these were killed. So I entered the building. I found the nails that we came to fetch. Everything else had been looted and this was only three days after my detention. All our belongings had been taken away. The doors were forcibly opened. I was deeply shocked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it that you finally left Susica camp for good?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left the Susica camp when the lists were prepared, so the group of people were on a list and these people were transported. They were told they were to be exchanged. But we left on 28th June, we were also told before we left and a friend or, rather, an acquaintance, Milof Marcic, told me that we would be exchanged. So they read out our names off the list and they said "You will be taken and exchanged." Then you were taken between the file of people and as we were boarding the bu we were beaten. Then again we were supposed to put our heads down, not to see anything, and so we spent some six to eight hours in the bus. But there was no exchange. When we came to our destination they -- when we came to Batkovic, in front of the hangar in Batkovic, they said: "Now, welcome to Batkovic. This will be pleasant for you", they said. "Nobody will beat you; you will do some work" but again we experienced the same kind of treatment as before. For me, in fact, it was worse than in the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a group of detainees at Batkovic who were specially singled out for maltreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Among them, I was one of those, and during the first three days they beat us. I was beaten and also Smajlovic and Sapardi and Ado, and this Ado was a strong, stout man, and the beating was very bad. They said -- and he asked me before he beat me, he said: "Why is your name circled red?" because my name was circled red on the list. So they said: "Ah, ha, that is because you were manufacturing knives and scissors", I do not know what, "allegedly preparing for the war". So they started to beat me. Also a man that had been working with me, this other man was accused of having driven a military vehicle, and the first two or three days they were beating us for a long time, for five to six hours, and we were beaten by some 10 people at one time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the guards give you a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as I arrived they called me "The Master of the knives" or the "Serb cutter" and they said you had a smithy at home and you were cutting knives o manufacturing knives. As time went on, each time they regarded us as extremists. So there were some 17 such people who were beaten every day two to three times a day, sometimes even more than three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten every day two to three times a day for that length of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was specially singled out. Every day for two to three times, after breakfast, after lunch, after supper, and during the night, around 1 or 2 o'clock in the early hours of the morning, they would take you out and beat you. And this was the particular group of some 11 to people who were specially singled out for maltreatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any injuries from these beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my left ear is damaged. My two jaws are broken. I have lost seven teeth above -- my upper lip was cut. Two, my two ribs were broken, the clavicle and the left -- left, something, damaged -- left foot, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the ICRC ever come to Batkovic? By ICRC I mean the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did arrive. I do not know the exact date, but we were hidden, some 10 to 17 people that I am talking about were hidden, because we -- and they continued to beat us every day. Not even my father could have recognised me, and the same was true of the others in the same group. They were hidden. They were hiding us from morning till evening. We were taken out in stables about a kilometres, up to four kilometres in the forest. The Red Cross detected us or discovered us probably in the month of -- I forget which month now -- and my brother who was with me, he actually -- he actually gav my name so I got the name of "Amir" although it was not me who actually spoke to the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why it was that they removed you when the Red Cross came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were hiding us so that they could continue beating us, because the Red Cross probably would not allow the beatings to go on. So they said that we, some 10 to 17 of us, were probably regarded as most dangerous, and people in the guards, in the guards, and each one of us was singled out, so that it was known which people were being beaten but the Red Cross could not find us. We were badly beaten, tortured, and I remember that one morning they came to us on the 11th September and they took some 10 of us and they decided they would take us for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, they searched us although I had nothing on me anyway. I only had a blanket, I think. So they searched us, and then there were black cars, the black moriah, the cars that was closed, totally closed, without any air. There we found a man from Srebrenica and we were driven for four or five hours. Then they opened the door for us. In the meantime, we had actually no air in the car. Then the man who was with us, a man by the name of Bricak, then they lined up the 11 of us and said: "This is Bircko". Some people wanted to beat us, but they did not allow that. Then they told us to enter the car again. The door was closed behind us, and then we were driven again for three to four hours again. I know very well that at on point the car stopped in front of a hangar. I did not know which town that was, which place that was, and we came out of that car sweating, and I always had two pullovers. This was useful because that dampened the blows. So they started beating us immediately. Some 20 people were there, armed with weapons with rifles. So we ran; came to a hangar and they started beating us again, and they told us to get in into the hangar and then we learned that we were at Doboj. There were already some five to six prisoners detainees already there. That was in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many other detainees there were in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from us 11 what were brought there, there had already been five to six people there, and from day to day they would bring new people. So that there were some 50 people, usually from Doboj and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the camp in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed there for -- until the 6th July 1993. Then they were told -- they told us that we would be exchanged at Batkovic, and that exactly is what happened. We were brought to Batkovic. We were exchanged. But before that we were we spent some 15 days in Batkovic, so that actually on the 21st July the exchange took place. I must say I never believed I would be exchanged ever because these were the kinds of people that you could not trust at all, and nobody should trust them ever.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not have any more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want to ask whether this continuous beating you suffered was particularly meant to a certain group, o was it a general attitude against all the detainees, and why were you sometimes singled out, in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me try to explain it because in Batkovic we were singled out. They regarded us or called us extremists and they said we had prepared for war, although none of us had prepared. I knew very well some 700 to 1,000 people that I know, and only two of them I know as fighters and I do not know. I was told later that Dragan Nikolic actually circled my name because anybody who was -- whose name was circled in red was then singled out and beaten. So there were some 17 people whose names had been circled, and so we had this special beating treatment, so to speak. But the others who were not like that, they had been treated badly as well; at least 10 blows received by any, every person, no matter old he or she was. There were people over the age of 80 who were also beaten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Berbic, could I ask you something? Regarding the camps, did all the prisoners have the same status? Was it the case that some of the prisoners were given the role, the specific role, of being intermediaries as regards the authorities or the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I have understood on the basis of some of the testimonies that, for example, some of the prisoners were grave diggers, and they had to repeatedly carry out that function and bury the dead. So my question is more general now. I am asking you whether a particular number of prisoners had specific roles, for example, as intermediaries in order to discuss working and livin conditions with the authorities or were they all treated in the same fashion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends. There were some men who under pressure, under pressure from Serbs, there were cases of Muslims beating Muslims. There were also Croats there too. They sometimes beat other prisoners, they were forced to beat other prisoners, by the authorities. They even brought civilians to beat us.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you. No other questions. I do not think any of us has another question. The Tribunal would like to thank Mr. Berbic for his testimony. I hope you will find inner peace and serenity in your future life. Could you please accompany him before we move on to the next witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Counsel for the Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honours, I have not myself personally spoken to the next witness who has, I understand, just arrived, but I have had Mr. Dixon speak To the witness. He tells me that the witness wishes to give his evidence in public with the exception of the address of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] So we will lift the order of disclosure partially and we have taken note of that and the decision of the Tribunal except, of course, the address of the witness. Could you tell us who the next witness is please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Sead Ambeskovic. I call Sead Ambeskovic SEAD AMBESKOVIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Do you hear me? Are you getting the interpretation? Mr. Ambeskovic, first of all, you will read out the oath which has been given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, only the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Be seated. Mr. Ambeskovic, we would like to thank you for coming to The Hague to give us your testimony. We are fully aware of the courage you had to have to come here. We hope you will feel at ease here. Bear in mind that you will have serenity because you are in a judicial circle, you are in an International Criminal Tribunal. It goes without saying if you have any difficulties, please do not hesitate to communicate it to us. Counsel for the Prosecutor you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases. Your full name is Sead Ambeskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Sead Ambeskovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a nickname by which you are also known?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Sajo", they call me "Sajo".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19th April 1966.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to 1992 where had you lived for the most part of your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vlasenica. I was born in Vlasenica and lived all m life in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your service were you then in the military reserve from 1986 until 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the reserve units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your employment in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a heavy machine operator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to cast your mind back, if you would, please, to 29th May 1992 in the evening at about 8 o'clock. I understand that at that time Dragan Bastah came to your house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Tribunal what happened when that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came to my house. I was there with my family. I was not -- I did not dare go out because they started arresting people around the town. So I did not have the courage to go out. I was with a friend too, Hajrudin Osmanovic, who was also staying at my place at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They surrounded my house. He came, Dragan, and three more individuals with him. They started knocking my door, and using abusive language, offending my nationality and religion, and told me to get out of the house. We normally went out at the door. I did not know what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who these people were that came to you house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not because I was in the house. I did not know what it was all about because I did not dare go out. I had not gone out previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went out of the house. They forced us out in front of the house, told us to put our heads against the wall and stand against the wall and they started searching us. They were asking for weapons, trying to find weapons. They could not find anything. Then they started to beat us. They asked for weapons. I could not answer anything because I had no weapons on me. I just had no weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these men dressed? Could you describe the clothes they had on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the four of them had the camouflage uniforms on. So they looked like special units, members of special units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Special units of what, the military or the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most likely it was their military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that they told us to go in front of the car. It was raining. We were not dressed adequately. We did not know what it was all about and we had to go practically without any clothes on and any footwear. Then they forced us to go into the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police station was near the bus station opposite the municipality building, the municipal administration building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vlasenica, yes

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you were taken to the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us into a room. It was a closed room. They closed the door and there was a leather upholstering on the door. There were a couple of other people there whose names I do not remember, and these four came with us, came into the room. The four of them then left. There were four people when we came in and they stayed, and those who had brought us had left. They started beating us and swear at us, offending our religion, and kept asking us where the weapon was, who was selling the weapons and who opened weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With what were they beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat us with truncheons, rifle butts and various wooden objects, mostly like handles, like pick handles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what part of your body were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat us on the back, on the head, and the area of the kidneys in the back, in the lower part, in the small of the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With what did they beat your kidneys with, in the kidney area of your back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly with rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just describe as best you can how they struck you with the rifle butts? Stand up if you feel that is easier to do it that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Demonstrated) Using all their force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this beating last for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It lasted about 30 minutes, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after the beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that they stopped beating us because we almost fainted, we almost lost our consciousness. They -- one o them got out, brought some paper and a pencil and told us to write who had weapons, where our weapons were and who had been selling weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. I could not answer that question. I could not write because I did not know. I was just not part of that, and so I was not able to write anything about anybody who had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they do anything to you when you did not write anything down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They started beating us again. They started beating us again, also with handles. Because we had been beaten, we could not take many more hits, blows, so they -- we fell down and they started kicking us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you fell down, where did they kick you? What part of body did they kick you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stomach, the chest, the head and also the legs too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the shoes that they had on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had classical army boots. Standard classical army boots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this beating last for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That lasted for about 15 minutes. A little bit longer, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After they beat you this time did they then say for you to write again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all the time they kept saying: "Write, write down", and they abused us verbally and they said: "You will have to say in the end anyhow."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that they went out for a moment. They left u there. We had almost lost our conscious and they brought some water for us to regain our consciousness. After that they ordered for us to be taken to the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then taken to the Susica camp once they gave that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately we were taken in a Golf, in a car of the make Golf, a police car. We were taken to the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of the men that took you to the Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Dragan Stanic, he was the driver, and he was accompanied by Golijan, Nedeljko Golijan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were met by Dragan Nikolic at the very entrance to the camp. Dragan Nikolic was there, Luka Majstorovic also, and two other men whose names I do not know, and I did not know them at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Dragan Nikolic prior to seeing him at the camp on that particular day or evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had known him. Frequently, before all this happpened, for about three or four years I used to go to his house. We visited each other even. I knew him quite well, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any particular circumstances that caused you to go to his house from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion when I went to see him, I went with my brother who was a mechanic, a car mechanic, I went there to help him with his car. I was there all the time and then after that we socialised frequently together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, just to clarify, the car that was repaired wa Nikolic's car; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was Nikolic's car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw Nikolic at the Susica camp when you first arrived, can you describe the way he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as I saw him, when we came there, he was in this colourful camouflage uniform. He had nothing, no cap on his head, but he did have insignia on the sleeves of his uniform. This was the Serbian tricolor, the military tricolor for the Serbian army. Also, he had a knife hanging from his belt, he had a pistol and in his hands he had a baton, and that is what he had in his hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen as soon as you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as we got off the car they started beating us. They also swore. They spoke abusively, swear words, referring to our mothers and say: "You are in our hands now, and now you will see what you have to confess."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember what it was that you were beaten with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic had a baton, as I told you, the rest of the guards had rifles, and the two people who were with him had rifles, Majstorovic was one of them, and Nedeljko Golijan was the second one. They had rifles and they started hitting us with the rifle butts and they actually -- and they actually beat us all the way to the guard, to the guard house or to their office, you might call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Nikolic himself beat you on this occasion with his baton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Personally, he hit personally. As soon as I got off the car he started swearing at my mother, my Muslim mother, he said, and said: "I will be interrogating you here and now you are in my hands". H started hitting me and then those that were with him continued, and it went on like this until we came to their office or to their guard house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember the date that this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the 11th June, probably at 7.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, they brought us into their office. They asked our names and dates of birth. Then they took us to what they called hangar and then we spent the rest of our time in that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they took you and searched you, did they take anything from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we entered the hangar, as we were entering at the gate, they stopped us and they took my watch, they took my driver's licence, they took my car regulation licence and the money that I had on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much money did you have on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had some 10 billion old dinars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they took it, who took the money and the other things from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was done by Dragan himself. He searched me. He took my belongings, he took my watch and actually he took everything that I took out of my pockets. So, I had to hand over everything to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened when you were put into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hangar, when I entered the building, I saw quite a number of people already there. I could not decide how many people were there, but later I learned that there were all together 700 people in that building. And I sa not far from the door because this was the only place that was free where I could actually sit down on the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any lighting in the hangar at night time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was one lamp which was some three to four metres from the door, and this was on a beam and there was an ordinary bulb hanging from there. This was a metal wire and that was four to five metres from the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the people that were in the hangar that you described, can you say whether they were all men or women or a mixture of both, or were they adults or children or a mixture? Can you give us a description of the ages and sexes of the people contained in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were some elderly people, there were some children and women. In the back part of the room there were men, while women were closer to the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much space was made available for people to sleep or to sit down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was not much space left for lying down. Actually, we were lying practically one on top of the other, so to speak. The hangar was full to capacity, and there was very little space so that they could walk, that the guards could walk so, like, a passage was left free so they could walk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given anything to sleep upon or lie upon when you were staying in that hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing. They did not give us anything. I was lying on the concrete floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about ventilation, were there windows in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were windows, but they were not open. The whole -- there was only one window that was open and tha was close to the door from the -- this was open, the upper part of that window was open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown the plan of the camp? (Handed). Would you look at that for me, please, and can you tell me, do you recognise what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the exhibit be placed on the machine? Mr. Ambeskovic, looking at the exhibit as it is on the machine itself, can you describe the features of the camp as you see depicted on that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These are the two hangars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you point to them with your pen. Thank you. That one you are pointing to, that hangar there, the first one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the hangar where we were staying, the one I am pointing out now. This is the guard house. There, I would say, their office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who stayed in that guard house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Dragan Nikolic and another man who was his clerk or his secretary, you might say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the place that you were first taken to when you arrived at the camp when Dragan Nikolic questioned you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the place. That was the place where we were first brought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other building, the other black hangar that you first pointed to, not the one where the people were, what was that used for, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I was never inside and I could not see anything special. This was simply some kind of military depot. There was some kind of military material there. There were no people there

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pointing with your pen, do you see the pole that carried the length electricity lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the electricity pole. That was the electricity pole where we were brought and beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking towards the back of the camp behind the hangar where the detainees were kept, there are two small buildings. Do you know what they were? You can perhaps point to them too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were like toilets put together with boards, wooden boards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The smaller building behind the storage hangar going immediately back and across from where the two toilets you pointed to, what was that building for you are now pointing at, what was that used for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was an old -- that was a shed for various kinds of military utilities. This was like a utility room for objects that remained and that was open. You could actually see inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fence you see around the camp -- and would you point to the fence for me, please, with your pen ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was the fence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- what was that constructed of? What was that made of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was barbed wire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The black river or creek depicted in the foreground of the camp on the plan, did that river or creek have a name that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the Susica. This is the River Susica. It was -- there was a bridge there. The River flowed under the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what this camp was used for prior to the wa in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I actually built that camp. We were digging the foundations, my company built. The hangars were used for the military material so as to be kept as a military depot. Later it was used for -- as a detention camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am now about to move -- I am finished with that exhibit, thank you -- on to another topic, but I notice the time. Is it now a convenient time, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Yes. Quite clearly, we were going to stop at 5.30. However, it is not exactly perfect to interrupt the witness. How long would the rest of your questions last, do you think, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Another hour, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] One hour. Then we adjourn hearing until tomorrow at 10 a.m.. (The proceedings adjourned until the following day) 25
